#4190. How To Complete Dodongo's Cavern In The Ocarina Of Time Remake

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has officially launched, so grab your Hylian Shield, load up your Fairy Slingshot, and get ready to save Hyrule once again. Throughout this journey, you will need to complete several dungeons that are filled with traps, puzzles, combat encounters, and a unique boss at the end.

One of the first dungeons you'll be tasked with completing is Dodongo's Cavern, which is located right outside of Goron City. This is a far more elaborate dungeon than the previous Great Deku Tree and will be your first real challenge if you're new to this title. If you're struggling at all or just want to ensure you find all the collectibles inside, here is how to find and do everything in Dodongo's Cavern.

After going through the massive hole you created on Death Mountain's Trail, you will enter a smaller room with a breakable wall at the back. Since we're currently limited to Bomb Flowers, grab one of the two Bomb Flowers and throw it at the rocky entrance to blow open the door to the actual dungeon. Step inside to trigger a brief cutscene introducing Dodongo's Cavern.

Dark Link is even more of an aura farmer than ever before in the Ocarina of Time remake.

Now that we're in the dungeon, you will want to head to the left side of the Main Chamber. Be careful as you traverse across the platforms, as they not only sink into the lava below, but you'll also need to contend with the new Beamos enemies. These foes fire a laser in a straight line that chases after you. You can either outright avoid them since they cannot move or destroy them with a Bomb Flower.

Make your way left and destroy the Beamos with the nearby Bomb Flower. Once it's dead, take the Bomb Flower and destroy the destructible wall near the back left corner of the room to reveal a large chest that contains the Dungeon Map inside. Additionally, you can use the Bomb Flower to destroy the other breakable wall on the left side to find a small chest that has a Blue Rupee in it.

After getting the Dungeon Map, head to the right side of the Main Chamber, taking extra care to not get attacked by the Beamos in the center. Just like before, grab the Bomb Flower and use it to destroy the Beamos on the right, before using it to blow open both of the breakable walls on either side of the elevated section.

In the back right corner will be a Gossip Stone, and the path forward will be in the bottom right corner. Progress down the tunnel and kill any of the Baby Dodongos that come scurrying out of the dirt. These explode a few seconds after taking damage, so always try to keep your distance from them after you swipe at these foes with your sword.

There's a Gold Skulltula you can get once you are playing as Adult Link. Return to the hallway with all the Baby Dodongos and look along the northern wall about halfway down the tunnel. Above you will be a Scarecrow point you can reach with the Hookshot via the Scarecrow Song! We can't do anything about it now, but it's good to come back to!

Once they're dead, approach the door with the stone switch in front of it. Push either of the two Armos Statues on top of the switch to permanently unlock this door. Progress through the hallway with the two Keese and go out the door on the other end.

When you enter, the door will lock behind you, and you'll need to kill two Lizalfos.

These enemies are quite nimble and will only attack you one at a time. Play defensively and use your shield to block their attacks before swiping at them with your sword a couple of times. After one takes a few hits, it will run away, and the other will take its place. Repeat this process of blocking their initial strike and counterattacking when they stop. There's no point in chasing after them, so just stay on the platform you entered on until both are defeated.

With the Lizalfos dead, a chest will spawn with a Red Rupee inside. You can also refill your hearts by hitting the pots on either side of the arena. Go into the next hall and use the Bomb Flower to blow open the cracked wall on the right. This will reveal a Business Scrub who is selling Deku Nuts and Deku Sticks if you need them. If not, progress into the blue-colored chamber directly ahead of you.

Make sure to have the Hylian Shield for this dungeon! If you have the Deku Shield equipped and take fire damage, it will burn up, and you'll need to get a new one!

In this room, there will be three Dodongos, which are slow-moving but relatively dangerous enemies. Their weak points are their tails, as the rest of their bodies are heavily armored. Approach one and wait for it to breathe fire before running behind it and slashing at its backside. Hit it twice and then back away to avoid its tail swipe move. Repeat this process two more times to kill the Dodongo.

Now, you do not need to actually fight these Dodongos if you want, but it does make the small puzzle in this room easier if you're not being harassed by angry lizards. Once they're dead, take out a Deku Stick and light the three unlit torches in this room. There will be one by the closest and farthest pillar, with the third being against the right wall.

This will unlock the door, letting you go inside. You're now back in the main chamber, so step on the stone switch to unlock the door directly across from you. Jump back down into the main chamber, head across the moving platforms, and go into the newly unlocked door.

Proceed into the next chamber and use a Bomb Flower to blow open the breakable wall directly to your left. Inside will be three Armos Statues, with one sitting directly in front of the ladder. Upon interacting with the Armos Statue by the ladder, it will come to life and attack Link. Equip your Deku Nuts and use them to stun the enemy, freezing it in place. Now quickly grab a Bomb Flower and throw it at this foe to kill it. Don't stand too close, as it will explode when it dies.

Approach the ladder and climb it to reach the chest that contains the Compass.

With the Compass and Dungeon Map acquired, the next task is to acquire the Bomb Bag so you can carry and use Bombs wherever you want. Upon leaving the room where you got the Compass, head over to the large stone pillar that is surrounded by Bomb Flowers. You'll notice a gap in the middle, so grab the lone Bomb Flower that's off to the right side and place it in this opening.

When the Bomb Flower detonates, it will cause a chain reaction where all the other Bomb Flowers around the pillar will explode in sequence. If done correctly, all the Bomb Flowers should explode, causing the pillar to shift, revealing that it's actually a staircase. Climb up the stairs and continue up the dirt incline until you reach the next door.

Gold Skulltula 1 — Bomb Flower Staircase Room (2F)

Your first Gold Skulltula in this dungeon is located at the top of the room where you formed a staircase via detonating all the Bomb Flowers. At the door, turn around and face the large wall that has netting on it. There will be both a normal Wall Skulltula and a Gold Skulltula. Use your Fairy Slingshot to kill them both and climb up to get your token.

In the next room there will be two Fire Keese and four Armos Statues surrounding a central platform. Use your Fairy Slingshot to kill the fiery bats and then approach the platform in the center. Three of the four Armos Statues around the platform are hostile, with the only inanimate one being in front of a ladder. All the hostile ones will have broken ladders behind them, so check for the one that has an intact ladder, pull the statue away, and climb up to activate the switch, opening the door.

Go across the bridge above the Main Chamber and kill the Fire Keese flying around you. In the next room there will be two spike traps moving horizontally across the ground between the series of pillars. Time your movements carefully and go to the back right corner. Grab the movable block and push it towards the lower pillar near the ladder.

Use the block to reach the pillar, which will let you both access a small chest that has some Deku Seeds and a Bomb Flower. Grab the Bomb Flower and toss it at the cracked wall by the ladder to clear a path. Now move the block in front of the ladder and use it to climb up to the opening you just created.

Continue into the next room where there is a large flame blocking your path. Take out your Fairy Slingshot and shoot the eye above the door, behind the fire to temporarily stop the blaze. Quickly cross the platforms and go into the next room. There will be several Baby Dodongos buried in this room, so carefully deal with them as you cross the lava to the door in the back left corner.

The next room will have two more Lizalfos that you'll need to deal with. Just like before, use the Hylian Shield to do your best turtle impersonation and wait for the Lizalfo to attack. Once it hits the shield, the enemy will be briefly stunned allowing you to get a couple slashes in before going back on the defensive.

Use this method to defeat both Lizalfos to unlock the doors and spawn a small chest. Before proceeding, go to the far end of the room and make your way through the narrow gap in the rocks. There you will find the newly spawned chest which contains a brand-new item called a Business Scrub Seed. When used, this seed will spawn a Business Scrub anywhere in the game, allowing you to buy items you might need. When you're done, head through the unlocked door on the left side of the Lizalfo arena.

In the next room, you will need to once again shoot the eye switch to make the flames on the platform cease. Hit the eye switch directly across from you first, then jump onto the platform that no longer is lit. Quickly look to your left to see a second eye switch and use your slingshot to also shoot this. Doing so will cause the second platform's fire to vanish, letting you safely cross.

You will then reach a room with a large chest which finally contains the Bomb Bag. This allows you to carry up to 20 bombs and use them anywhere you want! Blow a hole in the wall behind the chest with your newly acquired explosive and continue into the Main Chamber.

Now that we're back in the main chamber, we need to make our way to the boss' room. Step onto the switch to activate the platform on the ground floor to turn into an elevator between the different levels. If you want another Gold Skulltula, take the platform down to ground level, otherwise, go to the suspension bridge over the Dodongo Skull.

The second Gold Skulltula can be found in the side room to the southeast by where you were first introduced to the Armos Statues. In the hall that had the Baby Dodongos you will find a cracked wall that you can blow open with a Bomb. This will reveal a small chamber with a Gold Skulltula and three normal Keese.

Gold Skulltula 3 — Suspension Bridge (2F)

Another Gold Skulltula can be found to the right of the switch you used on the second floor to turn the platform into an elevator. Next to the suspension bridge over the Dodongo Skull, use a bomb to blast open the breakable wall and head inside. There you will find two Dodongos around a large rock. Kill the enemies and go to the back of the rock to find the next Gold Skulltula.

Once you're done getting all the Gold Skulltulas, head onto the suspension bridge over the Dodongo Skull. There will be two conveniently bomb-sized holes in the bridge that are above each eye socket. Drop a bomb into both eye sockets of the skull to light up the eyes and cause the jaw to open, revealing a new door you can go through. There will also be an additional bombable wall that has a small chest behind it that contains a Blue Rupee.

Make your way back down to the first floor of the Main Chamber and go through this newly opened door.

Upon entering through the door in the skull, make your way down the hill and then go up the incline on the other side. Ignore the switch on the floor for now; we will come back to it. Follow the path until you reach a room with several stone blocks. Grab the stone block directly to your left and line it up with the one on the raised section.

Doing so will let you climb onto the block you moved and push the one on the raised section to the area below. Now, head down to where you pushed the block and drag it to the back left corner of this room. Move your block so it's aligned with the one in the wall. Climb onto the block you've been pushing around and shove the one in the wall forward so you can reach the next section.

The final Gold Skulltula in Dodongo's Cavern can be found in the block room. Before you push the block embedded in the wall, move the block on the ground so it's in front of the cracked wall. Drop a bomb on top of the block so it blows open a hole to a side room. In this new area, you will find a hostile Armos Statue and three Baby Dodongos. Kill all of them, and you can find the Gold Skulltula along the back wall.

Follow the path back down to the room with the switch and push the stone block in front of you onto the lower level. Then drag the block into the conveniently block-sized hole with the switch at the bottom. Dropping the block onto the switch will unlock the boss room door.

The big bad of this dungeon is the massive dinosaur, King Dodongo. This hulking behemoth is far easier than he actually looks. Your main weapon during this fight will be bombs, so make sure you have a few before dropping into the hole you make in the boss's room. When you hit the ground, a brief cutscene will play that introduces the boss.

Right after you regain control of Link, equip the bombs and wait for King Dodongo to begin sucking air and fire into his mouth. Throw a bomb at his mouth while the boss is sucking in air to make him eat the explosive. This will detonate inside King Dodongo, stunning him and causing him to collapse onto the ground.

Quickly run over to King Dodongo and begin slashing at his tongue to damage him. Keep it up until he stands back up and closes his mouth. Now, run to any corner of the room and stand on the edge near the lava. King Dodongo is going to start rolling around the arena, but you can entirely avoid this attack by just hanging out where the lava and ground meet.

Once he slams into a wall, a few Baby Dodongos will spawn and rush towards you. Deal with enemies and wait until King Dodongo begins sucking in air once again. If you're fast enough, you can throw a bomb into his mouth and kill the Baby Dodongos, but if not, you'll need to avoid the massive fireball he launches. This projectile will ricochet around each side of the room.

Nothing else in this fight will change, so keep throwing bombs into his mouth, attacking his tongue while he's stunned, and using the edge of the arena to avoid his attacks. The only difference is he will summon more Baby Dodongos the second time he recovers from being attacked. Otherwise, this is an extremely straightforward fight.

After killing him, he will roll into the lava and turn to stone. A Full Heart Container will spawn, so make sure to grab it before stepping into the light and teleporting outside of the dungeon's main entrance.

And nearly 850 times the size of the original.

#4189. Diablo 4’s next class is the Warlock, but you can sort of play it today in Diablo 2: Resurrected’s new DLC

Blizzard has officially unveiled the Warlock, the second class coming to Diablo 4 with Lord of Hatred.

Diablo 4’s segment in the big Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight was among the biggest, even if the reason most of us tuned in was somewhat spoiled earlier in the same livestream. Blizzard unveiled the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The first class, being the Paladin, is already available to play for anyone who pre-ordered the expansion, but the Warlock won’t be accessible until the expansion arrives in late April.

The Warlocks are positioned as the opposite of the Paladins, in that they don’t mind utilising forbidden knowledge, drawing on the powers of Hell itself to fight its own overlords. The Warlock is the edgy, antihero counterpart to the Paladin’s purity and devotion to the Light.

The livestream did not show off any Warlock gameplay, but Blizzard is planning a dedicated livestream to show off the new class’ gameplay, and dig deeper into its lore and abilities. That show is scheduled for March 5.

What we did get to see was our first look at Skovos, the expansion’s new region. This Mediterranean-inspired location is where the new story arc will unfold, but it’s also being positioned as the endgame destination for Diablo 4 once the credits roll.

Lord of Hatred, of course, as previously revealed, introduces two new endgame modes in War Plans, and Echoing Hatred.

War Plans lets you create a custom playlist of up to five endgame activities to target specific rewards and create your own experience. There’s a new activity tree that works with all endgame activities, and creating War Plans is how you earn progression there.

Echoing Hatred, on the other hand, is a rare event that pits you against legions of Mephisto’s minions. It’s triggered through a rare lootable item that unlocks access. It’s essentially horde mode; where you’ll face unending waves of enemies, though not without a couple of twists.

We also got a bit more colour on the expanded class skill trees, which all players will benefit from when the expansion arrives. The Talisman system, which unlocks set bonuses, was also shown off. And, of course, the return of the iconic Horadric Cube, which gives you control over Affixes.

The Anniversary Spotlight should’ve had a Year of the Warlock subtitle, because the class is also making its way to both Diablo Immortal, as well as Diablo 2: Resurrected. The showcase revealed the Reign of the Warlock DLC, which adds the aforementioned Warlock to D2R - its first new class in 25 years.

Reign of the Warlock, which is available now in D2R, also makes a few updates to the game, such as new quality of life features, the Colossal Ancients endgame encounter, updated Terror Zones and more. You also get some cosmetics in Diablo 4 if you purchase this expansion.

#4187. The Elder Scrolls VI Has An Official Subtitle And It's 'Sentinel'

The headline tells the story: The Elder Scrolls VI has an official subtitle and it's Sentinel. So the full game is now titled The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel, or, as we will undoubtedly refer to it moving forward, as we colloquially do with the previous three games (Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim), Sentinel.

The news comes from Bethesda's various social media accounts, which are all sharing the video above. Along with the video, music, and the title, it also shares the text as a quote attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest to High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell (4E 206): "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate."

Sentinel is one of the nine major kingdoms within Hammerfell and is the capital of both the Alik'r Desert region and the Myrkwasa region of the Alik'r (source: elderscrolls.fandom). With this knowledge, it's fair to assume Sentinel will have many desert locations.

The name continues the tradition of naming the games after locations in the Elder Scrolls universe. Oblivion is the sort of exception, as it is a realm, but it still counts. We still don't know exactly when The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel will be released, but we're now about seven years from its original announcement at E3 2018.

#4186. Watch the Battlefield 6 Season 2 gameplay reveal here

As promised, our first look at the next Battlefield 6 and Redsec season is nearly upon us.

After a one-month delay, we’re finally days away now from the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 of live service. The second season is being revealed today, following weeks of teasers, and some Battlefield Labs testing of the first new map arriving with the new season.

It’s all going to kick off with a gameplay reveal, which is set to stream live later today.

As we’ve come to expect, the Season 2 reveal will take place via a YouTube premiere. It’s set to kick off live at 8am PT, 11am ET, 4pm GMT on the official Battlefield channel on YouTube - and embedded below. Today’s reveal will also be followed by a more detailed roadmap of Season 2, which will give us a much better idea about the volume and cadence of content we can expect.

Season 2 goes live February 17, kicking off a new chapter in the continued conflict between NATO and Pax Armata. The medium-large new map, Contaminated, will be available immediately at the season’s launch. Contaminated takes placed in the mountains of Germany, centered around a once NATO-owned airbase.

VL-7 psychoactive smoke appears to factor majorly into the gameplay of this new season, though we’re waiting to hear more details on that. We can expect new weapons, new gadgets, and the awaited return of the AH-6 Little Bird helicopter.

Look forward to more coverage from us as more details are revealed later today.

#4185. You Can Preload Grand Theft Auto VI On PS5 and Xbox Next Week, And You'll Want To Because It's Massive

We're just over two weeks away from the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, which recently graced the cover of Game Informer. Ahead of its November 19 launch, Rockstar Games has announced that digital preloading for GTA VI will begin next week on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

More specifically, preloading on Xbox Series X/S will begin Tuesday, November 10, at 12 a.m. GMT (4 p.m. PT/7 p.m. ET on November 9), and on PS5 at midnight local time in your time zone. Although Rockstar isn't producing physical discs of GTA VI, you can still buy a physical box at retail, which includes a download code for the game. The studio says, "Code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12."

The preload file will require 212 GB on your device, so make sure you have the space before you start the download. You can find more details about this process here.

Elsewhere in today's GTA VI news, Rockstar has revealed that on November 19, it will add an official printable GTA VI cover art poster and a map of Leonida as a free digital download to the game's official site. However, a double-sided physical version of this poster will be made available shortly after the launch of GTA VI from the Rockstar Store. It will only cost $0.99 on its own, or come free with any other purchase from the store.

GTA VI launches November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

#4184. Review: The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (Switch 2) - A Stunning Remake, But Not Quite Definitive

You’re not ready for this. No matter how many trailers you’ve watched or how much pre-release footage you’ve pored over, walking out into Hyrule Field for the first time in the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a revelatory experience.

It’s easy to forget how impactful Hyrule Field really was in the N64 original. While the game itself is still held in remarkably high regard, its main hub world has arguably been supplanted by later entries, particularly Breath of the Wild's enormous, immersive open world. It’s pioneering, yes, but it’s also quite small and empty when viewed through a modern lens.

The remake, with its breathtaking visuals, modernised controls, and revamped soundtrack, makes it feel new again. Standing at the entrance to Kokiri Forest and panning the camera around to soak in all of the details, I had to take a beat to stop myself being overcome by the enormity of the moment.

Making everything feel new again is really at the heart of the Switch 2 remake. I want to be clear: this is basically the same game, but Nintendo has tweaked just enough to make it feel fresh. Whether it’s the slightly different chest location for the Kokiri Sword or the Cucco hiding spots in Kakariko Village, there will always be something — however small — to give you pause.

The biggest change is the visuals. Much like Star Fox, Ocarina of Time is a staggering upgrade over the original, offering an almost overwhelming amount of detail across the board. From the small trinkets on Link’s tunic (who, by the way, is definitively 'Link' here, with no renaming options) to the way shards of broken pots stay on the ground and move underfoot, every aspect has been overhauled to take advantage of Switch 2’s power.

Yet despite the almost hyperrealistic visuals, it retains the original's spirit. There was a lot of discourse about the presentation when the remake was first properly revealed, particularly around characters’ faces. Any doubts about the approach will fade away as soon as you start playing. Everything looks right; whether it’s Link’s design or Zora's Domain, this is Ocarina of Time through and through. If you’re one of the many fans who were hoping to see the Spaceworld 2000 and Wii U tech demos properly realised, this is it and more.

The visual upgrades extend to the dungeons, of course, and it's crazy how impactful they are on your enjoyment. Inside the Deku Tree feels like a living world with realistic bark walls and copious spider webs. Likewise, the shimmering reflections and ethereal soundtrack completely transform the Water Temple. Despite minimal changes to the gameplay and structure — minor alterations to puzzles ultimately have little impact — the dungeons are a joy to explore once again.

It’s not all perfect, though. Keeping such a stunning game running at 60fps on a handheld takes some jiggery-pokery, and Nintendo's solution has resulted in a few visual blemishes. Assets in the distance — mountains and trees — look overly smooth and there’s some shimmering going on when you pan the camera around. It’s nowhere near as severe as Xenoblade Chronicles X on Switch 2, but it’s definitely something you’ll notice occasionally, particularly during handheld play.

Overall resolution takes a notable hit undocked, too, to the point where even Link himself can look a little fuzzy at times. It definitely needs mentioning, although it wasn't significantly detrimental to my experience. Keeping the game running smoothly feels like the more important priority, and Nintendo has nailed that aspect.

The audio has also been completely revamped, as well. The soundtrack, while familiar, has been reworked with new orchestral renditions, and everything from the Kokiri Forest track to the final, epic battle sounds incredible. Key cutscenes also feature voice acting, and it's some of the best I've heard from a first-party Nintendo game in quite some time. Your fairy companion Navi, whose in-game interruptions have been drastically cut down, is delightfully cheerful.

Exploring Hyrule and taking in the new visuals is made all the more satisfying thanks to the new control scheme. I’ve mentioned panning the camera around a couple of times, but it’s worth stressing that full camera control is completely new - a strange thing to highlight in 2026, but the ability to properly absorb everything this world has to offer really enhances your relationship with it. You feel so much more involved, and it helps that locations like Hyrule Castle Town have been upgraded to take advantage: no more pre-rendered backgrounds, you can now soak in all of the glorious detail.

The other major addition is the ability to jump whenever you please. Again, how quaint! Yet leaping at the press of a button gives you so much more autonomy over Link’s movements, even if it doesn’t open new routes or opportunities during your quest. You still jump at the same moments to scale platforms and solve puzzles, but doing it yourself without having to run off a ledge to trigger it is both quicker and more satisfying.

Combat feels comfortingly familiar: you lock onto your enemy and slash at them with ‘Y’, altering the direction of your swing by tilting the left analogue stick. You can hop about, perform a backwards somersault, and execute a leaping attack with either ‘X’ (the default jump button) or ‘A’, while holding and releasing ‘Y’ triggers the spin attack. It’s basically the same – why fix what isn’t broken, right?

Yet every attack now lands with such ferocity — accompanied by a searing red flash and a deafening crash — that combat feels completely overhauled. Again, old is new. Indeed, it’s so effective that it even makes Tears of the Kingdom's clashes feel comparatively tame.

Making use of your various weapons and items is also much easier than before. By holding down ‘R’, you’ll bring up an item inventory that instantly looks familiar if you’ve played TOTK or Echoes of Wisdom. Displayed in a single line, you quickly scroll left and right for your weapon of choice, whether it be a Deku Stick, a Bombchu, or the Megaton Hammer. The selection is relatively limited compared to, say, Echoes of Wisdom, so I never felt the UI was unwieldy or overwhelming; I always found what I was looking for straight away.

Meanwhile, key items like the Ocarina, masks, and Iron Boots are mapped to the D-pad. The latter is especially useful in the Water Temple, which gained its reputation as a major sticking point partly due to the need to repeatedly access the main menu to equip and unequip the boots. Tapping down on the D-pad is a lot more intuitive and makes for a breezier experience.

You can also do this for the newly-designed Lenses of Truth, which function exactly as the original Lens of Truth but have been revamped as a pair of goggles instead of a magnifying glass. It makes so much more sense!

The game is littered with similar tweaks, many of which have a noticeable quality-of-life impact. Reloading now drops you in the exact location you last saved (instead of at your house as Young Link and the Temple of Time as Adult Link). Elsewhere, the new Echo Gem, a reward from the House of Skulltula quest that replaces the Stone/Shard of Agony, shines and vibrates as you approach any Gold Skulltulas.

As for the Ocarina, you can play tunes in a variety of ways, the most basic of which is by simply pressing specific inputs via the face and shoulder buttons. Holding down ‘ZL’ brings up a menu of songs you’ve learned so far - handy for a quick reminder at any given moment.

However, you can also use the Switch 2’s built-in mic to input tunes using your own voice. Simply hum the tune you want and it’ll mostly pick it up with no fuss. You have the option to practice tunes if you wish, and it makes for a cute, if gimmicky way to use the Ocarina.

I’ve not been able to test Hori’s Electric Ocarina (and who knows where Nintendo’s official instrument is at), but I whipped out my guitar to test a few songs, and lo and behold, it actually worked. It certainly won’t be my go-to method, and chances are I’ll just stick to the buttons, but it’s neat.

I've not been able to test the Zelda Notes features during the review period, but you might find it a worthwhile addition if you're keen to create and share Ocarina songs. If you have some Zelda-themed amiibo lying about, tapping one during gameplay yields a few bonus items (arrows, recovery hearts, bombs, etc.), but thankfully nothing that could be deemed essential. All welcome additions, though.

What hasn’t been added for the remake is the Master Quest, and this is a real bummer. Available via a special GameCube release and as an unlockable in the 3DS remake, Master Quest proved an excellent way for veterans to test their skills upon completing the game. Given how closely the Switch 2 remake sticks to the core structure of the original, veterans will breeze through with minimal issues. And if you do ever get stuck, the new Threads of Time feature, which essentially documents your progress, will help you get back on track.

I died just once during the entire journey because I just got caught off-guard by an Iron Knuckle in the Spirit Temple. You can increase the difficulty slightly by altering the UI to show either minimal information or no information at all, but it’s no replacement for the changes that Master Quest could have brought. I'm hopeful that it will be added via an update, but it’s a glaring omission.

The lack of multiple save files is also disappointing. Yes, you can just create additional profiles at a system level, but the game allows you just one manual save along with several autosaves. Sometimes you just want to experience the start of the game again without impacting your main save file, so this is a shame.

The one last major addition is The Hall of Fallen Foes, and this is a cool, albeit inconsequential bonus. Accessed by sleeping in a bed after a specific campaign moment, here you can gaze upon statues based on enemies you’ve slain. It’s a lovely way to properly appreciate their updated designs, and you’re also given the opportunity to replay boss fights or even take on multiple bosses in succession. The rewards for doing so are useless, but the act of optimising your battles and beating your time is fun enough on its own.

And so, even with all that knowledge, you're really not ready for this. The visuals, the gameplay, the audio – everything has been thoughtfully upgraded to such a degree that this will completely replace the original for many. While the lack of Master Quest means it falls short of being definitive, it's still a remarkable remake, and a must-buy for Switch 2.

Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is a stellar reimagining of the original, one that completely revamps the experience with stunning visuals, modernised gameplay, and vastly improved audio. Despite some minor blemishes, this is comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time.

That said, it is a very safe remake. Despite lots of minor changes throughout, it’s still essentially the same game you’ve likely already played, and so you might find it offers little challenge if you’re familiar with the N64 original or 3DS remake. This makes the lack of Master Quest — or really any kind of hard mode — particularly glaring, but I’m hopeful it’ll be added in the future.

Subtlety is a premium, everything has to be glammed up. It's like an overcorrection for the excessive drabness.

There's no hero mode either. A remake should have at least a hook or two to get the original players a little excited. Just want to point out that I feel pretty confident that we would have possibly the same level of vitriole (maybe from the other side of the argument?) if this score had been a 10/10. It feels like every time this site or IGN releases a perfect score, they are criticized for being corporate shills, Nintendoters, lazy reviewers, etc. So, let's please be respectful and kind, take a couple breaths, and try to have some perspective. I know it can be frustrating to feel like your favorite/beloved [blank] isn't getting the appreciation or glory or credibility you feel it deserves - I was hoping for a 10 here, too! - but it doesn't have to take anything away from the enjoyment of it. I guarantee you are not alone with your love and passion for these media. But let's also try to understand that we - the people writing these reviews, included - are all individuals with subjective points-of-view. Everyone else's opinions are just as valid as your own. "It’s not all perfect, though. Keeping such a stunning game running at 60fps on a handheld takes some jiggery-pokery, and Nintendo's solution has resulted in a few visual blemishes. #4183. You're not crazy, trying to heal in Nioh 3 sometimes doesn't work - and Team Ninja is fixing it

One of the more insidiously aggravating bugs in Nioh 3 makes it so the game ignores you when you try to use elixirs, but hopefully not for long.

Nioh 3 has received a hot new update that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest update, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for update 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

This is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an issue that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into issues with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s update takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an issue that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

#4182. Afterwords – Marvel’s Wolverine

We interviewed game director Mike Daly after the launch of Insomniac’s recent Wolverine game to get his take on what makes Wolverine and Spidey different to work on, his thoughts on breadcrumb trails, and why Logan can’t ever seem to get the girl.

Insomniac had extensive experience working on well-known superhero characters before starting on Wolverine. Early on, what traits or qualities of Logan as a story character and playable avatar did you know you wanted to focus on, distinct from the Spider-Man games and character?

From a story perspective, we wanted Logan to be a man with centuries of experiences that he can’t remember, creating a mix of being worn, wizened, and cynical. His resilience makes him fearless, which comes through in his candid manner, and he can’t ignore his sense of justice, as much as he would like to.

For gameplay, it was important that players felt the difference made by his healing factor, claws, berserker rage, animalistic strength, enhanced senses, his adamantium skeleton, and corresponding weight.

In both story and gameplay, emotionally and physically, Wolverine is a hero who gets hurt and feels that pain deeply but always gets back up again and presses on. This dogged resilience was really important to us and a central theme of story and gameplay.

Wolverine is more of a linear adventure than the open-world exploration of a big city seen in Spidey. In my playthrough, that added to the sense of relentless pacing that characterizes Wolverine as a fictional lead. Was that part of the thinking behind why the game was built that way, or was the more linear path there for other reasons?

Ultimately, we made a game suited for a Wolverine story that had comic book pacing – action and meaningful story development on every page.

We experimented with different structures and stories, evaluating from the perspective of: “Is this the best way to do Wolverine justice?” As the various things we tried didn’t feel right, we had to challenge our assumptions and look to our favorite Wolverine stories for inspiration, which led us to where we ended up – a story with momentum in which every beat felt authentic to the character.

Scenes and gameplay sequences that might have been fine in other games but didn’t strongly evoke Wolverine undermined the consistency of the fantasy we were trying to create, so we tried to keep things very focused.

After the game’s release, there was an active online conversation about some of the breadcrumb-trail guidance the game offers to lead you to pickups, or to mark the continued golden path of progression. What was the thinking internally about that design decision, and your take on the debate after the game launched?

Our thinking was that it was essential to make the player feel like they were empowered by Logan’s enhanced senses, a canonical mutant ability, enabling players to do things they could not with other characters. We wanted to weave that power into as many parts of the game as we could, so that if Logan could smell or hear something relevant, the player could see it too.

For collectibles, we wanted players to enjoy seeking out and spotting senses cues, enabling you to find things that would have been obscure to other characters. Using the cues, players can cover a lot of ground without feeling the need to scour, maintaining story and action momentum.

After the game launched, we saw feedback from players that interpreted senses as abstract designer guidance, along with a desire for options in how they approached exploration and discovery. Fortunately, we have been able to incorporate this feedback from players in our post-launch patches. One aspect we’ve improved is the scent trail’s organic presentation, so they give a stronger impression that they belong in the world rather than being an abstraction. For players that want to do more manual exploration, we’ve added options to remove the sense cues for optional collectibles, and one to make scent trails dimmer until the player requests a hint.

Ultimately, enhanced senses are still essential to creating an authentic Wolverine, and that’s still reflected in the cinematic and environmental storytelling of the game. I think it’s great that on top of that, players now have more flexibility in how they experience them.

As a longtime comics fan, I found Logan’s combat system especially exciting, particularly for the relentless forward momentum it provided. What do you think were some of the keys to nailing that dynamic, as distinct from other high-quality third-person action games?

There were a few key elements we wanted to get right - Logan’s resilience, rage, claw feel, and overall lethality.

For resilience, Logan’s healing factor needed to feel important for survival - a prominent element of the system. A natural starting point there was to try continual regeneration so you could outlast enemies, but that quickly fell apart as it incentivized the player to slow the pace of combat or even retreat for maximum advantage. Even though it was incredibly effective at enabling survival, it was also hard to notice by the player so it didn’t feel prominent.

The key to solving this problem was making a connection between rage and healing factor. The Last Stand mechanic is a healing surge that can happen when you lose all your health, themed as using adrenaline to keep Logan’s heart beating. This incentivized aggression and made a space for an up-close look at visceral healing.

Speaking of rage, it’s the backbone of the combat system where being an indicator of momentum is key. At the low end of rage, you don’t have the safety net of Last Stand, so your decision-making naturally biases towards survival; ensuring you prioritize threat assessment and defense. As you climb into the middle tier, you have the leeway to push your luck for longer combos or barrages that let you build up rage and get kills faster. Finally, you get to rage tier 3, where the quick decay of rage makes your rate of kills the top priority, so you might prefer to attack groups over ranged stragglers just for the improved kill density. Beyond the mechanics, we change the presentation of combat, especially through Logan’s animations and exertion to reflect his state of mind. The presentation and systemic incentives drive the player into a frenzy, just like Wolverine.

We invested a lot in the details of claw feel to make sure it was distinct from general game attacks. Claws shred, so we added locational body damage to our enemies to reflect that, along with a dynamic blood system where it globs together as it is spilled, splatters on contact with characters or the environment, drips down the walls, diffuses in the water, and other details. Many kills throughout combat are punctuated with custom animations with cinematic camera work that pushes in and frames the puncturing of claws into the body for a strong impression of the connection and weight of the puncture. Severing limbs on these attacks is an occasional reminder of how sharp Logan’s adamantium claws are. Reinforcing this is top-notch sound and haptics design, so each hit registers.

The last aspect I’ll touch on is lethality, the rate at which Wolverine is able to dispatch enemies and vice versa. We found that fights where enemies were more technical and could survive a lot undermined what players expected to experience as Wolverine, which was aggressively and lethally tearing through a lot of enemies. On the other hand, combat was less exciting if the enemies didn’t feel like a serious and deadly threat, and you didn’t feel like Wolverine if a little bit of caution could enable you to defend perfectly and avoid all damage.

These aspects led us towards encounters where you confronted large groups of enemies that were highly aggressive, to the point of feeling unfair. Enemies can’t believably go toe-to-toe with Wolverine alone, even world-class mercenaries, so their strategy is in group coordination, which creates a counterweight to Wolverine’s own rage-based momentum.

Marvel’s Wolverine draws in a number of characters from across the X-Men comic mythology, but notably makes no mention of some foundational figures of that fiction – Professor Xavier and Magneto. That, in turn, leads to dramatically different lives for characters like Jean Grey or Logan. Is the narrative you crafted an intentional exploration of a world where those figures weren’t present in the early days of mutant emergence?

I would say it was more of an exploration of the character than the world. We wanted a story where Logan is pulled into conflict not because he’s a crusader, but because there’s no other option. There are no X-Men to help. His growth as a person should be a challenging journey, which could go unearned if he was surrounded by wise, supportive, heroic characters pushing him in the right direction. In contrast, his dynamic with the members of Team X evokes his struggle. The adversity to personal growth is what makes it interesting.

Jean does end up being the person that pushes him in the right direction, and that works because they can relate to each other, having had similar struggles.

In several versions of Marvel storytelling, Jean and Logan share a special bond, but Jean ultimately chooses Scott Summers as a partner. But even without that barrier in your story, Logan still hits some roadblocks to love. Is Wolverine fundamentally a better character when he just can’t get the girl?

The way I would put it is that a Wolverine story is fundamentally better when you empathize with Logan’s pain and admire him for pressing on despite it. That goes for his emotional pain as much as physical. He’s a tragic character in this regard – all he wants is to be at peace but can never find it for long.

Wolverine gets to take on a lot of the “heavy hitters” of his comic mythology in different boss fights throughout the game. When you began development, do you recall who the very first character was that you decided he simply had to fight in your game?

Sabretooth. No character is a better foil for Logan. His inner turmoil and chaotic behavior helps illustrate Logan’s own inner beast and his struggle to resist it. Sabretooth’s strength and mutant powers also provide a mirror to Logan in combat, and his savagery creates shocking moments that leave an impression. We knew an epic confrontation with Sabretooth was going to be a thing from the start.

#4181. Feature: 25 Years Later, How Many Of These Original Xbox Launch Titles Have You Played?

From the original North American launch on November 15, 2001

Welcome to the month of Xbox's 25th anniversary! Xbox will be celebrating that milestone officially on November 15th, but before we get there, we thought we'd use the chance to highlight the very first games that ever launched on Xbox.

To do that, we're going back to the initial list of North American Xbox launch titles, of which there were 20 in all. Some of them are obvious standouts, such as Halo: Combat Evolved, Fuzion Frenzy, Dead or Alive 3 and Project Gotham Racing, while others are more obscure - Arctic Thunder, Dark Summit, Mad Dash Racing, etc.

Here's the full list of all 20 launch titles:

Now, of course, some of these games are still playable to this day on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, while others have always remained locked to the original Xbox. The likes of Project Gotham Racing, Shrek and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2x are highly-requested additions to the Xbox backwards compatibility library, but it seems unlikely they'll ever make the cut at this point - almost certainly due to licensing reasons.

However, you may not know that games like Cel Damage and Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee are still playable to this day on modern consoles, and they're still well worth checking out despite their age.

So, how many of these original Xbox launch titles have you played? Let us know down in the comments section below, and please do give us your recommendations with some of the obscure ones - NHL Hitz is still one of my faves!

#4180. How To Complete Lord Jabu-Jabu's Belly In The Ocarina Of Time Remake

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has finally been released, which means it's time to once again stop Ganondorf from taking over Hyrule. Throughout this adventure game, you will explore all manner of weird and thematic locations, but none are stranger than the inside of Lord Jabu-Jabu.

A massive fish worshiped by the Zora, Lord Jabu-Jabu is the game's third dungeon and can be one of the trickiest if you're a newcomer. So if you're struggling at all, need a refresher, or just want to make sure you don't miss any Gold Skulltulas, here's a full walkthrough of Lord Jabu-Jabu's Belly.

After being sucked in by Lord Jabu-Jabu, you will start in this fish's mouth. Before progressing, I recommend equipping the Deku Shield, as there's nothing to burn it up like in Dodongo's Cavern, and you can use it to reflect projectiles.

Speaking of, two Octoroks will attack you after taking a few steps forward. Use your shield to bounce their projectiles back at them, instantly killing these enemies. Now, equip your Fairy Sling Shot and shoot the glowing yellow switch on the ceiling to open the door ahead.

The next room will introduce you to another new enemy called Biri, which are electrified jellyfish. They will stun you if attacked while floating and are immune to your Deku Seeds. Because of this, you'll want to use a Deku Nut to stun and force them to the ground where they can be safely dispatched. Head through the next door when you're ready.

Upon entering, you will discover Princess Ruto, and a brief cutscene will trigger. After refusing your help, she will accidentally fall down a hole. Once you regain control of Link, jump down the hole and talk to her. She will concede to letting you help her, which means you get to carry her around!

Why aren't you excited about this? It's a great honor, or so I'm told.

Our first goal is to unlock the Dungeon Map. Grab Ruto and head through the door directly next to her. The next hall will be filled with bubble enemies called Shaboms, which are relatively harmless unless you touch them. Either run past or kill all of them before entering the next room.

Jump into the large empty pit with Ruto and toss her onto the ledge on the other side of the room. Step on the glowing yellow switch to raise the water level and swim over to the large chest on the left. Inside will be the Dungeon Map! Be careful, as two enemies known as Stingers will spawn. They are quite aggressive and can be killed via hitting them twice with the Fairy Slingshot.

Your first Gold Skulltula in Lord Jabu-Jabu can be found in the Dungeon Map room. After you raise the water, swim over to the vines directly across from the large chest and climb up to the elevated area. Kill the Gold Skulltula clinging to the wall to claim your prize.

Now that we have the map, rejoin Ruta by swimming over to the side you threw her up to, but don't pick her up just yet. Step up to the next hall to cause a Bari to fall from the ceiling. Just like the Biri, they are quite dangerous and cannot be directly attacked without taking damage. Instead, use a Deku Nut for now to stun it and give you an opening to strike. Be careful: when a Bari dies, it will split into three Biri!

At the end of the hall, there's another ceiling switch you have to shoot with the Fairy Sling to open. In the next room there will be an Octorok, so kill it and step on the switch to activate an elevator. This will take you back to the throat, so go through the door and bring Ruta to the main chamber where you initially met.

In the room where you activated the elevator, there's an underwater tunnel you can swim through that leads to a Business Scrub. Use this to resupply if you need any items!

Now that we're back where we started, take Ruto across the room and go through the door directly ahead of you (this will be north on your map). Be careful running across to the other side, as there are multiple Bari and Biri that will drop from the ceiling. Additionally, you'll want to avoid all the large pink circles on the ground, as these will open up and drop you to the floor below.

In the subsequent room, step on the switch directly to your left and bring Ruto into the room that unlocks. Set her down once the door locks behind you before engaging the four Stinger that emerge from the ground. Play defensively and use your shield to block when they charge at you. Once they hit the shield, strike them twice with the sword to land a killing blow.

When all four Stingers are defeated, a large chest will spawn with the Boomerang inside. This will be your main tool throughout the entire dungeon, so toss it around the room a few times to get used to how it moves. When you're ready, grab Ruto and head back out into what we will call the Connection Room.

Head back out into the Connection Room and use your newly acquired item to kill both of the Tailparsan in the room. When they're dead, go right and set Ruto down on the switch that's below the large pink tentacle. This will keep the door unlocked, allowing you to enter. Inside, there will be a large pink parasitic tentacle. Lock onto it with Z-Targeting and throw the Boomerang at the thinner section in the middle.

This will cause it to take damage, so quickly start strafing in a circle around the room to avoid its counterattack. Once it's done swinging, throw the Boomerang at it again. Repeat this process a couple more times until the tentacle is destroyed. Head back outside, pick up Ruto, and follow the blue tentacle down the hallway you just opened up.

In the next room will be the blue parasitic tentacle and a few Biri. Enter the room and focus on dispatching the Biri first, as they can be a real nuisance when fighting the tentacle. Do not stop moving once you start fighting, as the tentacle is relentless in its attacks and is surprisingly fast despite its size.

When all the Biri are dead, wait until the tentacle runs out of steam and rests on the ground for a couple of seconds. Use this opening to hit it with the Boomerang before resuming dodging its attacks. Keep this up until the tentacle is dead, pick Ruto up, and head back into the Connection Room once more.

Go down the hall and follow the green tentacle this time into the next room. Just like the prior two tentacles, deal with the enemies guarding it before shifting your focus to the main threat. When the green tentacle is dead, take Ruto out and go to the room directly next to the one you just left. Inside, there will be a ton of Shaboms, so use the Boomerang to kill all of them to cause a large chest to spawn that contains the Compass.

Follow the dissolving green tentacle back to the main room where you met Ruta. A brief cutscene will play that shows a new route opening up with the tentacle's destruction. Use the Boomerang to kill the Bari and Biri that drop from the ceiling and then fall through the hole that has just opened up.

Gold Skulltula 2 & 3 — Main Room, Lower Floor (B1)

After you drop down the hole, you open up in the main chamber, you will find one Gold Skulltula on the northern wall above you and another in the hall leading northwest. Use your Boomerang to kill both, then throw the Boomerang at the token to bring it back to Link!

With the Gold Skulltulas dead, take Ruto and head into the next room to the northwest. This will trigger a brief cutscene where she sees the Spiritual Stone of Water in the center of the room. Toss Ruto up to the stone, which activates the elevator she's on, taking her up to the floor above you. Unfortunately for you, a Big Octo will ride the elevator back down and attack.

This is your first real dungeon mini-boss, a theme that will appear in all future dungeons you explore. When the fight starts, equip your Boomerang and throw it at the Big Octo to stun him. This will cause him to become immobile and stop chasing you in a circle around the arena. Quickly run behind him and smack the green blob on his backside to damage Big Octo.

If you're not fast enough, don't worry; stay behind him and throw your Boomerang again to stun Big Octo and give you an opening to attack. After you successfully damage him, Big Octo will pop up on the other side of the arena and spawn several Shaboms. Focus on the Shaboms, as you have limited space to move, so it's really easy to accidentally run into them.

Continue using your Boomerang to stun Big Octo so you can slash at his weak point with your sword until he is defeated. So long as you manage the Shaboms and keep your distance from this mini-boss, you should have no trouble beating this enemy. When he's dead, step onto the elevator Ruto took and go upstairs.

With Ruto gone, we need to find where she has run off to since she has the Spiritual Stone of Water. After you take the elevator, go through the door and approach the two platforms in the room. They will come to life and damage anyone who gets close to them. Quickly use your Boomerang to stun both of them, allowing you to safely cross the room without being hit.

In the next room, you will see a floor switch that requires someone (or something) to be on it to keep the door unlocked. Since we don't have Ruto anymore, look to your right to see a small stone box. Run over, grab the box, and toss it up to the upper level where the switch is. Now climb up the vines and place the box onto the switch to unlock the door.

The next room has several Biri in it and a large column on the right side. Kill the Biri with your Boomerang and use the vines to climb up to the top of the column.

Gold Skulltula 4 — Outside The Boss Room (2F)

You can find the last Gold Skulltula in Lord Jabu-Jabu right outside of the boss room where the large column is. After defeating the Biri, you can find the spider clinging to the vines on the column, so use your Boomerang or Fairy Slingshot to kill this enemy. Now just climb up and claim your token.

While on the column, look towards the northwest wall to see a yellow switch behind the wall. Throw your Boomerang through either the right or left hole to curve it around the wall and strike the switch. This will cause the door to open, allowing you into the next room. The final room before the boss fight has no enemies and just some pots. Make sure you have your Boomerang equipped before going inside!

Introducing Barinade, the main boss of this dungeon. Unlike the previous two dungeon bosses, fighting Barinade is mostly about just whittling away at its defenses to expose the vulnerable core body. Barinade is also the most dangerous foe you've faced so far, as it has multiple attacks, many of which can strike you at range.

When the fight begins, keep your distance and equip the Boomerang. Barinade will begin firing laser beams from its upper tentacles, so staying on the move at all times will ensure that it always misses. Just like the three colored parasitic tentacles you encountered before, your first goal is to destroy the tentacles attached to the ceiling.

This is done by hitting the exposed, white colored sections of the tentacles with your Boomerang. You can do this by either locking onto to each tentacle and throwing your weapon at it or just manually aiming the Boomerang by holding down the left trigger. I personally prefer the latter since it's easier to hit them while on the move.

Once all three tentacles have been severed, Barinade will take exception to this and launch several large, electrified jellyfish around it. These will begin spinning around the main body and are completely immune while their electrified shields are active. Keep your distance and focus on avoiding the spinning jellyfish for now. Eventually, Barinade will tire itself out, and all the shields on the jellyfish will vanish.

Seize this opportunity and destroy as many of them as you can with your Boomerang. You can use your sword for this; however, there's a chance of the jellyfish shocking you if their shield activates while you are attacking them! Keep in mind, once the jellyfish lose their shields, Barinade will start firing its lasers at you again, so stay on the move while attacking!

After all the jellyfish are dead, Barinade will rip itself from the ground and begin charging at you at a high speed. It will be completely invulnerable while charging, so just run away from it to ensure you aren't hit. Once Barinade slows down, throw the Boomerang at the main, glowing orange body of the boss. This will stun it, causing the shields on the jellyfish to vanish. Just like before, take out as many jellyfish as you can before it resumes attacking.

With all the jellyfish destroyed, Barinade will finally be vulnerable to your attacks. In a final, desperate attempt to defeat you, Barinade will begin spinning around the room and firing lasers. Hit the main, pink body of Barinade with your Boomerang to stun it, causing the boss to fall to the floor.

Now run over to Barinade and start whacking away with your sword until it recovers. Back up and use the Boomerang again to stun the boss, allowing you to strike it once more. Keep repeating this until Barinade is dead, signaling your completion of the Lord Jabu-Jabu's Belly dungeon!

#4179. Genshin Impact Luna 5 takes the squad back to Mondstadt, finally makes Varka playable

Genshin Impact's next update will have you reminiscing about the good ol' days of... 2020.

The latest big content update has been revealed for HoYoverse's breakout game, Genshin Impact. Version Luna 5, which has the unusually long and needlessly layered title — Song of the Welkin Moon: Variation - Homeward, He Who Caught the Wind — is set to arrive February 25.

This one is a bit of a nostalgia play, taking everyone back to Mondstadt, the place where you may remember taking your first steps. And, as with any good return to the ol’ hunting grounds, come familiar characters, too.

The big new arrival is Varka, who joins as a playable character for the first time. Varka, Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius, is a character whose debut has been long-awaited. He is a 5-Star Anemo Claymore wielder with a dual-wield combat style, capable of dealing two different types of Elemental damage. His addition means that there's now finally a burly 5-Star male character of each elemental type... do with that information what you will.

Varka's dual-wielding combat style allows him to deal two different types of Elemental damage at the same time. The way it works is that his Elemental Skill boosts the damage of his regular attacks, but it also converts the damage type of his right-hand claymore to match his teammates’ elements (Pyro, Hydro, Electro, or Cryo). The left-hand claymore always deals Anemo damage.

The more normal attacks you use, the more frequently he can activate a special Elemental Skill, or trigger a Charged Attack that doesn’t consume stamina. He can also rely on the Hexerei effect to trigger more instances of Elemental Skill, as well as Charged Attacks, making him a monster damage-dealer.

Varka, of course, has been a staple member of the cast, featuring in both the original story in a small cameo, as well as taking a bigger role in the recent Nod-Krai chapters. With the return to Mondstadt, his playable debut makes sense. His Story Quest will shed light on his encounter with the Wild Hunt, and the Great Wolf King of the North

The reruns for this version are going to be Flins — who will be available in the first phase of Event Wishes — as well as Skirk and Escoffier in the second phase. You can also look forward to the return of the Chronicled Wish with Mondstadt characters.

Staying on the theme of reminiscence, the big event in Luna 5 is centered around revisiting memories from the beginning of your time with Genshin Impact, and reuniting with old friends. In Echoes of Memory, you’ll witness familiar scenes that have been changed slightly, and you’ll need to use the Spotter Kamera to detect and record those differences.

The Knights of Favonius are hosting several other activities for everyone to take part in, including an event that lets you catch up with old friends over drinks which you make for them.

Outside of events, there’s a new set of Gliding and Combat Challenges. And, of course, there are new minigames that you can relax with. The Kamera is being utilised yet again, and this time you can use to capture sights from your time in spots across Natlan, Fontaine, and Sumeru. There’s also… a horde mode of a sort, where you fend off waves of enemies.

Catch up on the latest set of Genshin Impact codes before you play, and check out why we think Genshin Impact is one of the best mobile games you can play today.
