#4178. Holiday Gift Guide 2026

With the holiday gift-giving season upon us, it’s time to think about the gaming fans in your life and find the ideal present to brighten their day. And if you’re the gamer in the family, we always encourage you to circle relevant items in the coming pages and leave your magazine open in hard-to-miss locations around the house. We’ve scoured dozens of tech products, tabletop games, collectibles, and more to select and highlight some of the coolest items we found this year.

We recommended the Board shortly after its launch, but with its expanded game library and lower price than first-adopter rates, this holiday season is an ideal time to make the leap. This family-friendly platform features original games that sit comfortably between the digital and physical divide. The horizontally placed screen shows the backdrop of one of the several included games, or the sold-separately add-on games that have popped in since launch. Each game has its own real physical play pieces that interact with the action onscreen, often in innovative and charming ways. Think of it as the best of both worlds between board games and video games, and you’ll get what they’re shooting for here. $399

Few additions to the latest Dungeons & Dragons rules pack as much punch and value as this new expansion, focusing on ways to develop further and evolve the use of magic across your tabletop gaming sessions. New subclasses, spells, creatures, magical items, and factions add thoughtful, intriguing options for both players looking to play someone new and DMs hunting for new story hooks and challenges. $50

If you’re as excited as we are about this month’s celebration of the Tomb Raider legacy (see p. 40), this centerpiece statue is an ideal fit for your collection. Standing roughly nine inches in height, Lara is poised for exploration in her original classic garb. The sculpt strikes a perfect balance between crisp detail and stylistic presentation, in line with that early version of the character; the metallic blue motorcycle paint is especially striking. $250

For players longing for the glory days of stand-up arcade games, it’s hard to beat Arcade 1Up’s approach. The team’s sturdy cabinets look and sound great as a marquee feature of your game room. The new Outrun machine features much of the original display art, a bright 19-inch screen, and responsive gas and brake pedals as you steer around those tight corners. Sega has packed in OutRun, Turbo OutRun, OutRunners, and Power Drift. If old-school racing isn’t your thing, look for cabinets that run the gamut from Pac-Man to Joust to Claw Machines. $629.99

The long-running Nendoroid figures continue to be an attractive but still affordable choice for building collections across numerous fan-favorite series. There are somewhere around 2000 characters at this point! New entries like the Genshin Impact collection make a strong case for the line. The look is chibi, the quality is excellent, poseability is high, and customizable face and accessory parts let you change up your display over time. $46

We’ve previously sung the praises of Libernovo’s versatile approach to an ergonomic gaming chair, which includes a lumbar stretch functionality, a steady recline option for comfortable pushback without sudden shifts, and dynamically adjusting parts as you move through your day. The Maxis line does all that, but addresses one of the fundamental problems for at least some users with the original – it wasn’t big enough. With features like a wider base and longer headrest reach, the Maxis aims to provide the same comfort to the players who are tall or wide enough to need the extra breathing room. $1119

If you’re the player on your team who likes to have easy access to soundboards and real-time voice changing, the Key Pocket could be just the ticket. This small device straps onto your phone for mobile play, but it’s also compatible with consoles, Discord, Twitch, or just about any place you want to tweak audio on the fly. A free tier gives you access to some voice-changing and sounds, while a separate subscription opens up hundreds of thousands of additional options. But be warned: we can’t help you after your friends abandon you for that baby voice you won’t stop using. $99

The question of the best bang for your buck in modern consoles has become extraordinarily complicated, especially as tech prices have soared in recent years. There’s no right answer, but Sony’s high-end machine walks the line of offering extremely high-tier performance without escalating to even higher-priced gaming PCs. Higher and more consistent frame rates than on standard PS5, advanced ray tracing, and an increasing number of games that feature enhanced PSSR image options all add up to a better gaming experience, if you’re ready to make the significant price jump. $900

If the gamer in your life is looking for a stylish, understated way to express their love of the hobby, Anicorn’s designer watch collaboration with PlayStation could be a standout option. Available in black and a slick silver/white combo, the minimalist timepiece includes the familiar face buttons of Sony’s controller encased in an oil-injection display so they slowly and freely float across the watch as you move. $250

It’s a safe bet you’ve at least seen the popular Shashibo puzzle cubes by this point. We’ve been fans of their brain-teasing, fidgety fun for some time. Battle Shapes takes the core concept – reshaping the box into various distinct magnetically-locked shapes – and extends it into a timed game experience, playable solo or head-to-head. By targeting specific shapes, you significantly improve your speed with the toy, and scannable QR codes on the cards offer clear tutorials for each shape so you can prep for competition. $50

While the vast majority of gamers looking for good personal audio are going to be okay with a larger set of cans over their ears, We know more than a few players for whom that’s a definite no – for comfort, awareness of surrounding sounds, or other reasons. The Arc 5 earbuds aim to solve for that, with an over-ear design that feels extremely comfortable. And because they sit on the ear, you can still hear what’s going on around you. While that limits some aspects of the final sound quality, the inclusion of THX certification, Dolby Atmos optimization, and Dynamic Bass Enhancement helps to ensure audio is still very strong. $230

Across Lego’s many recent themes, Tolkien’s legendarium has offered some stellar sets. The largest yet is the capital of Gondor, with an astonishing 8,278 pieces and a height of roughly two feet. The castle/city build is impressive, featuring tons of interesting angles and turns. The finished product aims to offer the best of both worlds in presentation – a microscale representation of the front façade and a reverse minifigure-scale Hall of Kings. We especially like the inclusion of Denethor’s cherry tomatoes. $650

The original Azul is often cited as a foundational entry in modern board gaming. The “Kids” versions of celebrated titles aren’t always a sure bet, but this one holds up to scrutiny. Azul Kids lowers the complexity threshold but keeps the foundational strategic thinking. Players lay out uniquely shaped tiles into mosaic frameworks in colorful, appealing patterns; the basic concept of the original inspiration is clear, and kids as young as five can grasp and enjoy the fun. $25

Many corners of the collecting world have embraced the fun (and frequent despair) of blind boxes, where you never know exactly who you’ll get in a given series. Funism has a strong track record for quality, offering adorable smaller figures like their latest line of Evangelion collectibles. Each figure stands nearly four inches and features both human characters and mecha. You can buy singles and roll the dice, or purchase larger sets with a no-duplicates guarantee, which can save a lot of heartache if you’re trying to line your whole shelf. $21

If you’re going to spring for a high-end keyboard for PC gaming, it’s important that you like the feel of the keys. The slightly smaller overall 75% size profile of this Blackwidow has no impact on the great feel of typing – a clear highlight for the unit. The customizable, colored backlights are also a big selling point, as is the side command dial and built-in OLED display, which can be tweaked to show PC performance, GIFs, lighting brightness, and more. It’s a strong contender in a crowded field, and justifies its price with both comfort and customizability. $300

Beautiful, vibrant art and a refreshing take on the classic area-control board game genre are the two strongest reasons to take a close look at Wroth. Players control one of five races vying for supremacy across a conflict-ridden peninsula. Factions are asymmetric, so everyone has unique capabilities, and that adds significant replayability. Players roll and draft dice, allowing distinct actions that move the game forward. And move it does; unlike many games of this ilk, Wroth can be learned quickly and played to completion in a little over an hour. $65

Console and computer hardware prices are skyrocketing with no sign of slowing, and perhaps as a result, retro gaming handhelds are gaining popularity. Many quality devices are available, but what sets the Evercade Nexus apart is its officially licensed game cartridges. Imagine the nostalgic joy of a Game Boy, but with a cartridge that includes both Banjo-Kazooie and Tooie. The cartridge boxes even include manuals. For fans of physical media, Evercade Nexus is a great option. $199

This tiny USB-C plug-in (with included USB-A adapter) solves a bunch of audio challenges in one uniform device. It offers high-resolution Bluetooth transmission on iPhone, high-bitrate audio transmission to compatible LDAC headphones, enables high-quality Bluetooth output from your PC, and even low-latency Bluetooth audio on PS5 and Switch. In short, it takes a huge number of products with a USB port and ensures a dynamic Bluetooth audio connection with relative ease. $99

The original MV6 is a familiar sight on streams thanks to its clear voice reproduction and overall ease of use. Shure has built on that success with the Gen 2, offering an excellent standalone mic that doesn’t break the bank. Available in black or white, the Gen 2 features a handy auto-level mode that keeps volume even as you adjust your own amplitude, an adjustable denoiser for your space, a longer cable for out-of-the-box convenience, and three presets for plug-and-play use. In short, it’s an excellent choice if you want great performance without needing an audio engineering degree. $169

XR Glasses are still fighting for awareness, but once you try them, it’s easy to see why the concept is on the rise. Viture’s Pro 2 makes an impressive case for adoption, with a competitive price point, comfortable wear, and a giant 146-inch screen that floats in front of your face for gaming or work on your PC or phone. The display is crisp, bright, and impressive, even as the glasses are light and easy to use. With a mobile dock mini (sold separately), you can even snap onto a Switch 2 with ease and start playing instantly. $299

Role-playing gamers have several excellent universal systems to pick between when considering a story or campaign idea that might fall outside traditional genre staples. Among many good options, Cypher stands out as one of the very best. The system uses a rules-light, narrative-focused approach that prioritizes player-driven storytelling across everything from hard sci-fi to superheroes to intrigue- driven espionage. This is the corebook that’s needed to run and play the full system; additional books only add options. $50

As gamers have continually migrated toward personal audio that can rock amazing sound without disturbing the whole house, high-end premium headphones have become a dangerously competitive space. Turtle Beach meets that challenge head-on, with a robust option that sounds beautiful in use. The Stealth Pro II boasts the slick ability to wirelessly switch between different devices, which is awesome if you’re one of those players who regularly jumps between platforms to play your favorite titles. Like the whole category, it’s a lot to spend on a headset, but Dolby Atmos, active noise cancellation, and 60mm dual drivers all add up to a powerful argument. $300

With an increasing number of top-tier console and PC games like Resident Evil Village, No Man’s Sky, and Dead Cells now available on iOS, not to mention the consistent quality of Apple Arcade, Apple phones remain the best mobile platform for gaming. The 18 Pro Max phone has implemented a number of tweaks that strengthen the platform, including higher memory, much faster graphics processing, impressive HDR performance, and notably improved battery life, all adding up to a gaming experience that is working hard to justify your playtime when away from home. Starting at $1299

SteelSeries is best known for its strong audio line-up, but its push into premium-tier controllers exhibits a similar flair for quality and usability. The new Aeon Pro has a lot to recommend it as your go-to Xbox, PC, or mobile choice. The two included batteries (one of which can always be charging in the dock) ensure essentially unlimited playtime. The full-pull or hair triggers and buttons are clicky and satisfying, and the Hall Effect thumbsticks are built to minimize any drift. Textured handgrips and overall heft are ideal. And an onboard OLED lets you adjust profiles and button assignments, switch between platforms, and check battery at a glance. $260

Valve’s pricey VR headset isn’t a revolution in the medium, but the company has been invested in the technology since its inception. As a result, the Steam Frame is a very good, very comfortable headset. Like its competition, the Quest, its best use is playing games locally on the headset, and Steam’s library is vast and interesting. Wireless connected play to a powerful PC is also well done, but currently the included Wireless Adapter is not fully compatible with the Steam Machine – a baffling limitation we were shocked to confirm. VR is an expensive sub-hobby within video games, but Steam Frame is among the best ways to explore and enjoy it. $1059

Many of the coolest “gaming lights” focus on the flexibility and fun of bright RGB customization. While we’re fans of that aesthetic, it leaves others out in the cold who might want something a bit more natural. The Elements hex panels feature a natural wood-inspired panel, customizable “scenes” like a campfire glow, and can react to both music and touch, with adjustable ambient white light to keep the vibe relaxed. $200

Kyle Hilliard contributed to this article.

#4177. Nioh 3 is, unsurprisingly, the fastest-selling game in the series with over a million units sold

Nioh 3 has taken the Nioh franchise to new heights, delivering its biggest-ever launch.

Even before the game came out, it was pretty easy to guess that Nioh 3 would be a hit. From the word of mouth leading up to launch, to the well-received free demo, there was little chance the action RPG wasn’t going to be a major deal.

Today, publisher Koei Tecmo has announced that the game has officially passed over one million copies sold worldwide across PC, and PlayStation 5. This makes it the fastest in the Nioh franchise to reach this milestone.

As a result of this fantastic launch, Nioh 3 has now pushed overall Nioh franchise sales to be over 10 million, which includes the original Nioh as well as Nioh 2. Today’s news comes just two weeks after the game arrived on PC, and PS5.

On Steam, where it’s available on PC, it shot up the Steam charts, and immediately broke the series’ previous best peak concurrent player count record. From there, the numbers kept growing, leading up to a stellar weekend where it peaked at 88,045 concurrent players on Steam, double that of its launch day.

This now stands as the largest for any Nioh game on Steam, and though we don’t have insight into how well it’s doing on PS5 specifically, it still shows that the Nioh series continues to grow.

Nioh 3 builds on everything the two prior games established, and pushes the series into the semi-open-world realm, with several larger maps that each cover a period of time in Japan’s history. In our Nioh 3 review we called it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.”

If you’re curious about the challenging and very rewarding action RPG, start with these gameplay tips, and don’t be shy to call upon a friend (or stranger) for help using our co-op guide.

#4176. Nintendo Joins The Accessible Games Initiative, Adopting A Bunch Of New eShop Game Tags

Nintendo has joined the Accessible Games Initiative and, in the process, has added a collection of new accessibility tags to the eShop.

The new tags — which include various accessibility features like 'Narrated Menus', 'Full Input Remapping', and 'Playable with Buttons Only' — make it easier to sort through games based on specific requirements. Simply select a tag from the eShop Tags page, and it will bring up every game where that requirement can be applied.

A product of the Entertainment Software Association, the initiative has also been adopted by Amazon Games, EA, Google, Xbox, Riot Games and Ubisoft. "Our goal is to improve players’ gameplay experiences by providing clear information about the accessibility features available in video games," the Accessible Games Initiative website reads.

Here is a full list of all the tags included in the project. You can find detailed descriptions of what each of them entails on the AGI site.

The eShop is intimidating enough as it is, so we always welcome new ways of sorting through its many, many titles to find a game that suits.

What do you make of these new eShop tags? Let us know in the comments.

[source accessiblegames.com, via nintendo.com]

#4175. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

#4174. Cover Reveal – Tomb Raider: Legacy Of Atlantis

Game Informer’s next cover story is Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis, the upcoming reimagining of the original 1996 Tomb Raider arriving on February 12. Since that game celebrates the franchise’s 30th anniversary this year, we’re doing the same with a double-whammy of Tomb Raider features.

We visited Crystal Dynamics’ office to play Legacy of Atlantis for several hours, including an exclusive tour of the Greece section. For our 12-page cover story, we spoke to key team members at Crystal Dynamics and Flying Wild Hog to learn why it’s tackling Lara Croft’s seminal adventure once again (having already remade the game once in Tomb Raider: Anniversary), how this version of the game differs from previous incarnations and why, discuss the teams' controversial use of AI development tools, and how Legacy of Atlantis plants seeds for the upcoming Tomb Raider: Catalyst.

The issue also includes a six-page retrospective of Tomb Raider’s 30-year history, with insights from Crystal Dynamics. This celebration is reflected in our cover art, designed by Tomb Raider franchise art director Brenoch Adams, which showcases every version of Lara Croft from the Core Design, Legend, Survivor, and current eras.

The December issue also marks the return of our annual (and very large) holiday buyers guide, featuring curated gift suggestions for the gamers in your life ahead of the winter holidays. Furthermore, we’ve created a list of family-friendly games to enjoy with younger relatives during upcoming holiday gatherings. Guest contributor Veerender Singh Jubbal writes about India's emerging game development scene and how its community is helping elevate local titles to an international stage. Ahead of the launch of Ryu Ga Gatoku’s Stranger Than Heaven, executive editor Brian Shea played a new section of the era-spanning Yakuza/Like a Dragon prequel while picking the brains of its lead designers for details on the game’s plot, themes, and time periods. Senior associate editor Wesley LeBlanc shares his glowing impressions of Murals, the colorful, fairy-tale-inspired adventure from Disney Illusion Island developer Dlala Studios, whom he spoke with about the game’s conception.

We also have plenty of previews for upcoming games including Final Fantasy VII Revelation, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV, Muramasa: Revenant Blades, Fate/Extra Record, Tiny Metal 2, Mr. Records, and Eternal Anima. We also have reviews for Gears of War: E-Day, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve, Control Resonant, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Silent Hill: Downfall, and many more.

#4173. OG Xbox Game 'Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee' Gets Remastered, But What Do The Critics Think?

Was it worth digging the original Xbox title back up?

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee launched on the original Xbox in 2003, a few months after its GameCube debut, and sadly, only in North America. The kaiju arena-brawler, which depicted the iconic King of Monsters, Godzilla, body-slamming Ghidorah into various cityscapes, has apparently made a big enough impact to warrant Atari funding a remaster in 2026.

Sadly, the whole North American release made it quite difficult for us Brits to get our mucky mitts on the game, and DAMM wasn't a big enough deal for Xbox to share the game with the rest of the world. DAMM did get the backward compatibility treatment, however, only on Xbox 360, and again restricted to North America.

I guess then, we're quite pleased Atari decided to take a punt on a DAMM remaster. Even though it seems to share many of the original's downfalls, Godzilla's WWE antics are going to be available on November 3rd on Xbox Series X|S, and best of all, I can play it from my lovely little home in Cornwall.

So, here's what the critics are saying about Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered:

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered brings the classic kaiju brawler roaring back with impressive rebuilt visuals, satisfying arena destruction, and chaotic multiplayer battles. While its limited roster and tedious character unlocks feel dated, the accessible combat and faithful Godzilla presentation make this a thoroughly entertaining return for the King of the Monsters."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered feels like a new game with its graphical upgrade, held back slightly by a lack of any other meaningful new additions and a somewhat grindy gameplay loop."

"Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a satisfyingly faithful update to a beloved Kaiju brawler. It’s simple and fun, with local and online multiplayer keeping you around for the long haul despite a wafer-thin single-player experience. Now if we could just get a remaster of Save The Earth and Unleashed."

Review Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (Switch 2) - The King Returns With A Fun But Thin Kaiju Brawler

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is at its best when it simulates the idea of smashing kaiju toys together as a kid in short sessions with friends, and at its worst when it attempts to prolong a game that never had much depth to begin with. The result is a remaster I’m glad exists considering the drought of Godzilla brawlers, but with a few caveats–not to mention the sting of realizing that the original GameCube and Xbox game were absent of arbitrary grinding."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered remains goofy fun, and Atari’s remaster looks and runs well. It’s still a rather simple game and probably not the most comprehensive when it comes to the characters and lore. But it’s a good time and offers quite a few different modes to get acclimated and beat up famous faces."

"Right now, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a great version of a good retro game. Because the game was remade from the ground up, I wish the developers had made a super version of the Godzilla trilogy with more content. While Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered’s combat is really fun, there’s not much depth. There are lots of modes, and a bit of RPG unlocking, but this isn’t a deep fighting game that’s going to be played at tournaments. It’s a great budget buy for Godzilla fans. But more content would have made Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered a more obvious recommendation. If you’re at all curious, or have any fondness for the original game, it remains a fun time."

"In the media shadow of sacred monsters like Grand Theft Auto VI and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, only an equally fearless monstrosity could face them: Godzilla. Nearly a quarter century after its release on GameCube, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee returns with a remaster that discreetly refreshes the audiovisual experience and improves the progression without betraying its structure. The core is that of a 3D fighting game in which kaiju clashes are accompanied by the destruction of entire cities, in a blaze of explosions and particle effects. Behind this chaos lies a combat system that's immediate, but not always precise and balanced, suspended somewhere between classic fighting games and the festive jumble of a party game. The mechanics are simple, despite a certain unwieldiness in the movements, and the best of the action is found especially in local multiplayer."

Well, there you have it, folks! Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is an almost perfect example of a good '7' rated game. At the time of writing, the remaster is holding down a 72 score on Metacritic.

What's interesting is that the original Xbox release scored 73 on Metacritic - a single point higher than the remaster. It's funny how 23 years can pass and a game can be reviewed almost identically.

#4172. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

#4171. How To Beat The Forest Temple In The Ocarina Of Time Remake

There are a lot of dangerous places to explore in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. From Death Mountain to Kakariko Graveyard to inside a giant fish, you'll venture into all manner of thematic locations.

One of my personal favorites is The Forest Temple, which is the first dungeon you'll complete as adult Link. However, it's not as easy as it sounds, as the training wheels are completely off. So if you're struggling to beat The Forest Temple, want to ensure you don't miss any Gold Skulltulas, or just want an easy time solving all the puzzles, here's a complete walkthrough.

Upon entering the Forest Temple, you will be immediately attacked by two Wolfos. These are aggressive enemies that strike at you with a three-hit melee combo. The trick to killing them is to perform a backflip right before they attack. This will cause them to miss, spinning them around so they face away from Link and expose the glowing blue weak point on their spine.

Kill both of the Wolfos and look towards the door that's chained up with a lock on it. Introducing a new dungeon mechanic you'll need to become very familiar with. Going forward, some doors will have these chains and locks on them, which can only be removed if you find a Small Key. These keys are finite and will be consumed upon using them on a locked door!

Look to your right at the large tree with all the vines. Use these to climb to the top and carefully make your way across the flat tree branches to reach the small chest. This will contain a Small Key, which we will use to unlock the door to the actual Forest Temple.

Gold Skulltula 1 — Forest Temple Entrance (1F)

Our first Gold Skulla can be found at the Forest Temple entrance. At the very top of the tree covered in vines will be a Gold Skulltula. Kill it with the Hookshot and snag the token.

Go down the hallway, kill the Skulltula that drops from the ceiling, and enter the Grand Hall. When you arrive in Luigi's Mansion the Forest Temple, four different colored Poes will appear and steal the fire from the torches that match their colors. Each of them will run off to a corner of the dungeon, and your goal is to restore the fire they stole.

In the Grand Hall, make your way to the door at the top of the stairs directly across from where you entered.

Conveniently, your next Gold Skullatula can be found near the top of the stairs on the north side of the Grand Hall. At the top of the stairs, turn to your right, and you'll see the spider clinging to the wall. Like the previous one, use your Hookshot to kill and take the token it leaves behind.

Going through the next hall will introduce you to a new enemy called the Blue Bubble. This adorable name is given to the giant flaming skull with bat wings, which will attempt to ram itself into you. Use your shield to block the attack, extinguish its flames, and allow you to land an easy killing blow. Once it's dead, go into the next room.

Oh look, more new enemies. This time the door will lock behind you, and two Stalfos will appear. These are the most dangerous normal enemies you've encountered so far. Boasting a shield and sword, these skeletons can easily block your attacks and perform big sweeping strikes. The key to defeating them is to wait until one performs a jump attack and dodge it. This leaves them wide open to be hit, but it will take several sword slashes to bring one down.

When both Stalfos are dead, a small chest will appear with a Small Key inside. Head back the way you came and return to the Grand Hall.

In the Grand Hall, look for a door with a large blue block in front of it. Stand next to the block, pull out your ocarina, and play the Song of Time. This will cause the block to vanish, allowing you to use the door behind it. Go through the door and kill the Deku Babas while making your way over to the wall on the right.

Use the Hookshot to kill the two Skullwalltulas and climb up the vines to the balcony. Look to the wall with the large archways, and you'll see a Hookshot grapple point above one of the balconies. Pull yourself over to it with the Hookshot, kill the Blue Bubble, and step onto the switch to drain most of the water out of the well below you.

Jump down the well into the water and run down the path to the chest to get a second Small Key. Climb out of the well and be ready to deflect a projectile from the Octorok in the small fountain. Once it's dead, use the grapple point on the pillar to pull yourself over to the large chest. Open it to find the Forest Temple dungeon map. Exit out the door behind you and step on the switch to raise the gate, putting you back in the Grand Hall again.

Since we cannot use the Fairy Slingshot anymore, we need to find a suitable replacement. In the Grand Hall, make your way to the red-colored side of the room and up the stairs to the locked door. Use a Small Key to open it and head inside. Go down the hall and enter the next room where a Blue Bubble and a third new enemy, the Wallmaster, await.

As you run around, you'll notice a colored circle appear at Link's feet. Keep running back and forth until the large, severed hand lands on the ground. If it hits you, the Wallmaster will toss you back to the Grand Hall, so make sure to avoid it! Once the Wallmaster lands on the ground, turn and immediately kill it before the monster can retreat. When it's dead, kill the Blue Bubble and head up the ladder.

Now, go down the narrow passage and take the second left. Walk along the balcony until you reach a door with a large block in it. Push the block into the hallway you just ran down so it lines up with the door. Get behind the block and push it down the hall with the triangles on the floor. Once you reach the end of the hall, run along the balcony side again and shove the block a final time so it's under the opening above you.

Do not go up to the next floor; instead, go to where the block originally was and climb up the ladder along the wall. Follow the path until you find another block and push it forward into the adjoining hall. Go back down the ladder, run to where you finished placing the original block, and climb up. Go to the block you shoved into the hall and push it towards the second elevated door. Use it as makeshift stairs, then take a right and use the ladder.

Kill the two Blue Bubbles and then use your remaining Small Key to go through the locked door. Make your way down the twisted hall and quickly jump across the gap to the door on the right. There will be another Wallmaster, but with such minimal space to move, you're better off just avoiding it.

In the next room, there will be portraits of the Red Poe, but ignore them for now. Head down the stairs and through the door to trigger another fight with three Stalfos. I know I shouldn't have to say it, but just to make sure: do not stand in the glowing green poison pit in the middle. Upon killing all the skeleton warriors, a large chest will appear with the Fairy Bow inside.

With your newly acquired Fairy Bow, it's time to hunt down that Red Poe, Jo. Shoot the eye above the door you entered through and go back into the staircase. Use the bow to shoot any painting with the Red Poe in it, but keep your distance; otherwise, the ghost will flee. There will be one painting at the top of each staircase and a third over the bottom of the lower stairs.

After the ghost is forced out of the paintings, she will retreat to the lowest level of this room. Go down the stairs and draw your sword. Jo's main attack sees her spin like a top in front of you, deflecting all attacks. The trick is to turn away from her to bait this move out, then quickly run out of the way once she starts spinning. At the end of the move, Jo will be dizzy and vulnerable to your sword swings.

Do this twice to finally kill Jo and restore the red flame to the Grand Hall. Three more Poes left!

Open the small chest that Jo left behind to find a Small Key and head back into the room where you found the Fairy Bow. Use the key on the locked door directly ahead of you and go inside. This will bring you to another staircase room where Beth, the Blue Poe, is located. Just like with Jo, use the Fairy Bow to shoot the three portraits that specifically contain Beth in them.

This will make her retreat to the bottom of the stairs where you can fight her. Similar to Jo, Beth relies on a spin attack that makes her dizzy if she misses. The catch is, Beth will repeat the spin twice in succession, so make sure to dodge her second attack! Once she is recovering, run over to Beth and start slashing away.

Remember, you can goad Beth into attacking by looking away from her. When you do this, she will physically manifest herself, allowing you to turn and attack when she gets close. Upon killing Beth, the blue flame will return to the Grand Hall and a large chest will spawn containing the Compass.

With her dead, go back the way you came through both the Fairy Bow Room and where you killed Jo. Head down the twisted hallway and go through the door. When you exit the door at the end of the twisted hall, turn around and look over the door. Use the Fairy Bow to shoot the eye switch to reorient the hallway so it's normal.

Go down the previously twisted hall and jump down onto the lower floor. A Wallmaster will attempt to grab you, so make sure to dodge its attack and kill it. Once the Wallmaster is dead, open up the very ornate chest to find the Boss Key! Don't get ahead of yourself though; we have some work to do before battling the Forest Temple boss.

Jump down into the hole next to the chest, kill the two Blue Bubbles, and proceed through the door. You will emerge on a balcony overlooking the garden where you drained the well.

Gold Skulltula 3 — Second Floor Garden (1F)

On the second floor of the garden where you emptied the well, carefully walk out onto the ledge to the left of the door. Follow it around the corner until you see the Gold Skulltula in front of you. Use the Hookshot to kill and grab the token.

On the balcony, take the first door on the right to enter a small room. Inside will be a Floormaster, which is a troublesome enemy. It will launch itself at you, so block with your shield and strike it down. When it dies, the Floormaster will split into three smaller versions that are going to try to latch onto Link. If they do, the Floormaster will recover and grow to full size.

You prevent this by quickly killing all three mini-Floormasters before they can grab Link. A spin attack works wonders here since its large radius lets you hit multiple enemies at once! With the Floormaster defeated, open the chest to get a Small Key, head back onto the balcony, and go through the next door.

This will spit you out into the block room. Go back up to where the entrance to the twisted hall is and shoot the eye switch again. This will contort the hall back to its previous state, allowing you to reach where you killed Jo and Beth.

You can get a Purple Rupee in the block room on the second floor by shooting the long eye switch. This will drop a treasure chest containing your prize.

Head back to the top of the stairs where you killed Beth and go through the door. Go up the ladder on the right and run down the hall with the two Green Bubbles. Kill both of them and use your Small Key to unlock the next door. In this room, you will find a frozen eye switch and an unlit torch. Step on the stone switch to ignite the torch, and then fire your bow through the torch. This will set the arrow on fire, melting the ice around the eye switch.

Now shoot the eye switch to contort the blue hallway, go back down the hall, and jump down the hole in the floor to the lower level. In the checkered room, when you get close, the ceiling will begin to rise and fall. Ignore this for now and head to the right and through the door. Push the block onto the ground and then go back through the door to the checkered floor room.

Your final Gold Skulltula in the Forest Temple can be found in the West Garden. After you've pushed the large block down to make a shortcut, look above you at the small balcony to see a Scarecrow spawn point. Play the Scarecrow Song to summon him and then use the Hookshot to pull yourself onto the balcony. There you'll find the Gold Skulltula.

Wait until the floor falls onto the ground and then quickly run to the stone switch on the right. Be careful, as there are several Skulltulas that will fall from the ceiling if you get close, so be on the lookout for their shadows on the floor! Once you step on the switch to unlock the door, wait until the ceiling rises again and go to the small chest to get a few Bombs.

Now run to the door once it's safe and go through. In the Poe Room, shoot the large painting of Amy on the wall. She will then cause her image to become split up across five blocks. You need to push those blocks together to form her portrait once again. The catch is that one of the blocks that shows the right side of her head is fake. Look for the image of her head to occasionally move, as that signifies which block is real and which is fake.

Once the blocks are pushed together to form her image, Amy will appear and attack. Just like her sisters, Amy will perform a spin attack. Unlike them, she can do it three times in succession. Wait until she gets dizzy from all the spinning, and then attack. Repeat this a second time until Amy is dead, and the green flame is restored.

Go through the door to directly enter a hallway with a portrait of the Purple Poe on the wall. Shoot the painting to force the Poe out of hiding, causing her to retreat into the Grand Hall. Follow through the newly revealed door and jump down to where the torches are to initiate a fight with Meg, the final sister.

Unlike her siblings, Meg isn't content just spinning around like a top. Instead, she will clone herself and try to hide among her copies. Stand in the center of the room and look for a Meg that is holding a torch with a purple flame. Pull out your Fairy Bow and shoot this Poe to stun her and force her to vanish.

The next set of Megs will all have unlit torches, except the real one, which will still have a purple flame. Just like before, shoot the real Meg with an arrow to make her retreat. Her final set of clones will all look exactly the same and have the same colored torch. This time, you want to pay attention to her movements. As they circle around Link, only one of them will do a little spin.

When you see the spin, shoot that Meg with an arrow. If you're not fast enough, she will attack you and then hide back among her clones. The best way to quickly determine which one is real is by positioning the camera so it's looking directly down at you and the four Megs (shown above). Once you hit the real Meg with an arrow, strike her several times with your sword to finally kill her.

With all four Poes dead, take the elevator in the middle of the Grand Hall down to the lowest level of the Forest Temple. Grab the horizontal stone pillar on the wall and push it once. This will cause the walls to rotate around the room, revealing a small chamber with a stone switch on the floor. Step on the switch to ignite the torch.

Grab the stone pillar and push it again twice to reveal a room with a small chest that contains some arrows. Then push the pillar a third time to reveal a green-colored room with a few pots and a Skulltula. This will also line up the torch with the frozen eye switch. Shoot an arrow through the fire to thaw out the switch, and then hit it with an arrow to unlock the boss's room.

Gold Skulltula 5 — Outside The Boss Room (2B)

The final Gold Skulltula in the Forest Temple is located outside of the Boss Room. Rotate the room via the pillar a total of four times until the green-colored chamber with the pots is accessible. Go inside and look up at the wall to find the Gold Skulltula.

The big boss of the Forest Temple is Phantom Ganon, who is a fake version of the real man. When the fight begins, Phantom Ganon will retreat into one of the large paintings while on horseback. Equip your Fairy Bow and begin looking at all the paintings around you until you find two of them that show Phantom Ganon riding straight at Link.

One of these is real, and one is fake. You won't be able to tell who the phony is until he is about to escape the painting. Right before they reach the end of the road, the real one will continue pushing through the painting into the real world, while the fake turns around to ride back to the castle. The moment the real Ganon begins to appear in the boss room, shoot him with an arrow to force him back.

If you're too slow, he will jump over you and fire a projectile that deals a decent amount of damage. Repeat this a second time, making sure to shoot the real Phantom Ganon as you emerge from the painting. Where things get tricky is that the third time sees Phantom Ganon appearing in every painting.

Keep spinning your camera around once he gets close to the emerging to ensure you can see the real one as it escapes. Shoot it with an arrow to finally force Phantom Ganon off his horse. Put your bow away and draw your sword.

Phantom Ganon will float into the air, create a massive orb of energy, and hurl it at you. Instead of dodging, smack the orb when it's close to you with your sword to send it back to Phantom Ganon. He will do the same and return the orb to you. Keep volleying the energy orb back and forth until it eventually hits him. When this happens, rush over to Phantom Ganon and begin hacking away with your sword.

Learning absolutely nothing, Phantom Ganon will attempt this same attack again. Just like before, keep returning his serve until the orb strikes him and knocks the boss to the ground. Slash him a few more times before he retreats into the air. This time, Phantom Ganon will not just summon an orb, but will launch himself across the ground in an attempt to skewer you.

When he initiates the attack, dodge to the left or right to avoid this move. He may do this move multiple times in a row, so be ready! Eventually, he will summon the orb for you to smack back at him once again. This time, you should be able to kill him before he can recover, so slash away with your sword until the boss is defeated. After a brief cutscene, grab your Heart Container and step into the blue circle, completing the Forest Temple!

#4170. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4169. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#4168. 'Too Big A Risk' - Game Developer Sparks Debate After Delaying Playtest Due To AI Concerns

Will it push us towards a more cloud-focused future?

As AI continues to adopt a bigger influence in the gaming industry, there have been concerns in some circles about how people can use AI to reverse-engineer games, including for upcoming titles that haven't even been released yet.

This became a particular talking point a couple of weeks ago when Moonlighter developer Digital Sun Games decided to delay a planned (PC) playtest for their upcoming game ReVamp, worrying that the code might be reverse-engineered before they actually had a chance to release the full game.

Here's what they had to say in a statement at the time:

This ended up sparking a whole bunch of discussion regarding developers that might choose to adopt the same strategy, potentially opening us up to a future where demos and trials for upcoming games will become less prominent.

Some even took it further, suggesting that reverse-engineering will push us to a cloud-focused future:

A few people pushed back in the comments, suggesting that games have still been successful despite the existence of piracy and other elements that have threatened their potential over the years, while others highlighted that stronger protections in the future may be able to limit the damage from reverse-engineering situations.

For what it's worth, it's been reported in recent days that Claude has begun blocking attempts to clone and reverse-engineer games, and it was confirmed by an Anthropic dev that the idea is to "steer it away" from recreating other developers' titles because infringing IP is against the company's usage policy.

Ultimately though, it's too early to know what the future holds, but it's an interesting topic of discussion at the very least. Don't be surprised if instances like this still crop up, and hopefully it's something that Xbox is actively thinking about.

#4167. Switch Cartridges Under Threat As Key ROM Manufacturer Exits Business

Move may accelerate transition to digital

Macronix, one of Nintendo's key ROM manufacturers for physical game cartridges, is ceasing the production of ROM altogether.

This comes via analyst David Gibson who relayed the news from Macronix's latest financial release. According to the data, ROM products accounted for just 5% of the firm's overall revenue for Q3 2026, representing a stark decrease of 39% year-on-year.

It will now shift its focus over to NOR and eMMC memory chips instead, and will no longer report ROM sales separately in its future financial releases.

Gibson is keen to stress that Nintendo will have other partners to utilise when it comes to the production of cartridges, but this move may nevertheless accelerate the transition to digital game sales alongside Game-Key Cards.

Digital sales have already made up more than 60% of Nintendo's total sales during Q4 2026 and Q1 2027, but this tends to fluctuate based on major game releases.

It'll be interesting to see whether Nintendo itself addresses this development in its own financial release, which it due to drop this week on 5th November. Even if it doesn't acknowledge it in its own material, it seems likely that the question will arise in the company's usual Q&A session. We'll keep an eye out and relay its reaction and plans going forward.

For now, it's likely business as usual for Nintendo, but we'll be interested to see just how this affects the production of physical cartridges in the future and whether it will indeed accelerate the transition to digital.

Update: There are conflicting reports as to whether or not Macronix supplies ROM for Switch 2 specifically. For now, we've removed the mention of 'Switch 1 & 2' from the headline and will investigate further. We'll update this piece as soon as we're able to clarify.

@Olliemar28 That 60% digital sales figure is a bit misleading since it also includes download-only games, DLC, and NSO subscriptions.

If you look at the data in the tables on page 23 of the Q1 2027 Financial Results Explanatory Document, you can do a bit of basic math to isolate out the digital-only games, DLC, and NSO subscriptions. This results in the following more granular breakdown of software sales revenue:

Digital versions of games available physically: 38.9% Physical games: 38.5% Digital-only games, DLC, and NSO subs: 22.6%

So if you compare digital to physical for just games available in both formats, it's basically a 50/50 split. Still higher than past years where physical was ahead, but digital is not as dominant as some would have you believe.

#4166. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4165. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#4164. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4162. Two Big Remasters Are Now Lined Up For Xbox On December 3rd

Including a first-ever Xbox appearance for the original Thief!

It's usually the case that December is a quiet time for new video game releases, but we've still got a few notable ones lined up for the first couple of weeks on Xbox, including two very interesting remasters on December 3rd.

We already knew about the first of these - Rayman Legends Retold is coming to Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S on that date. It seems a little bit redundant to "reimagine" an Xbox One game like Rayman Legends on the face of it, but the previews have been pretty great for the most part, and there's no doubt that Legends is a great game in general.

The next one has just been announced for December 3rd today though, and it's Thief: The Dark Project Remastered. The original Thief has never appeared on Xbox before, having first released on PC back in 1998, but it was considered one of the best games of that year across any platform, and has a whopping 92 average rating on Metacritic.

Its remaster is being handled by the experts at Nightdive Studios, known for an absolute ton of great remasters in recent years, so as long as you don't mind the dated nature of it, this could end up being a must-buy on the 3rd.

Exciting stuff! We'll leave you with more details on both games down below.

On this page: Two Big Remasters Are Now Lined Up For Xbox On December 3rd

Embark on a bold reimagining of the acclaimed platformer, filled with new content and narrative twists. When a shadowy villain spreads corruption across the Glade of Dreams, journey through its charming worlds solo or in up to 4‑player couch co‑op in a fast‑paced, side‑scrolling adventure where every stumble and surprise adds to the delightful chaos.

In Thief: The Dark Project Remastered, Nightdive Studios brings back the pioneering 3D stealth game from Looking Glass Studios. Described by its developers as a “first-person sneaker,” the 1998 title challenged norms with its non-confrontational gameplay at a time when most first-person games prioritized combat. Thief was the first stealth game to use light and sound as game mechanics to help you hide from and sneak up on characters, rather than simply attacking them. Remastered with Nightdive’s KEX Engine, the release includes Thief: The Dark Project and the additional missions, content and updates from the 1999 Thief Gold re-release.

#4161. God Of War Laufey Delayed To May

PlayStation first-party developer Santa Monica Studio has delayed its upcoming action game, God of War Laufey, to May. More specifically, the PlayStation 5-exclusive title will now launch on May 20, representing a roughly three-month delay from the original February 16 release date.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen," a statement from the studio reads. "We don't take for granted the trusted place in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans. With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20, 2027. We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey stars Faye, Kratos' deceased wife from his Norse adventures, after she ends up in the mysterious realm known as the Everywhen following her death. There, she will fight monsters and creatures from various mythologies alongside a talking gelatinous cube and a talking sword sash. We'll have to wait a bit longer than expected now to see what her adventure entails.

God of War Laufey will now launch on PS5 next year on May 20. In the meantime, check out this newly revealed weapon, then read about how Amazon's God of War TV series has recast Kratos as Dave Bautista.

Diablo 4's latest Developer Update is nearly upon us, and it's one plenty of the game's fans and players have been looking forward to.

Diablo 4’s next, long-awaited Developer Update finally airs today. This meaty livestream was first announced nearly a month ago, when Blizzard initially revealed that the game’s next class is the Warlock.

The Warlock’s initial unveiling, however, was incredibly brief, showing no gameplay. It also didn't explain how the class is going to fit within the existing roster. This all changes today.

The Warlock is one of two classes coming to Diablo 4 with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion. The first, the Paladin, is already available in the game for anyone who pre-orders the expansion. The Warlock will instead arrive alongside the expansion on April 28.

The Developer Update will also include a first look at the game’s next season (Season 12), currently set for March 10. This mini season will only last until the expansion’s release, so it’s going to be interesting to see what it brings to the game.

You’ll be able to watch the showcase live at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT on Diablo 4’s official YouTube, Twitch, and Twitter channels. We’ve embedded the YouTube and Twitch players below for your convenience.

Among the topics the Developer Update will cover are the Killstreaks system, as well as Bloodstained items. As always, you can also expect a Q&A segment at the end of the show, and I imagine there’s going to be a few about the Warlock.
