#4159. Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

Blizzard has unveiled the next Diablo 4 season, which kicks off next week to hold us over until the launch of the game's big expansion in April.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

#4158. Round Up: The Reviews Are In For The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time On Switch 2

The week is finally upon us, folks! We are less than 24 hours away from the launch of Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, and to say that we're all excited would be an understatement.

Our excitement is made all the bigger by the fact that the game's reviews are now in, so we can start to get an idea of what the full experience has in store for us.

Here at Nintendo Life, the sublime Ollie Reynolds awarded Link's latest a 9/10, calling it a "very safe remake," but "comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time". Here's a brief snippet followed by a link to the full thing:

The visuals, the gameplay, the audio – everything has been thoughtfully upgraded to such a degree that this will completely replace the original for many. While the lack of Master Quest means it falls short of being definitive, it's still a remarkable remake, and a must-buy for Switch 2.

Review The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (Switch 2) - A Stunning Remake, But Not Quite Definitive

But of course, we're not alone in our thoughts. Reviews have now gone live across many outlets, so we have assembled the following roundup to give you an idea of the spread of critical opinions as it stands (spoiler: there's not all that much of a spread).

We'll start with a few full-beans scores. The first comes from GamesRadar, with a 5/5 review that calls it "a reimagining bigger and bolder than any I've ever played before it":

It's as timeless as it ever was, managing to recreate one of the most beautiful games to date without compromising the magic of its 1998 predecessor – only adding to it

VGC also came in with a 5/5, praising "how little has been lost in translation" between the remake and the original:

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was already one of gaming’s most essential experiences, and this wonderful restoration makes it the definitive way to discover – or rediscover – a masterpiece

And Eurogamer followed suit with another 5/5:

This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday

Things drop ever so slightly (perhaps thanks only to the bump to a bigger review score range) in Game Informer's 9.25 review:

I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry

By approaching this remake with a degree of reverence and respect for the source material, Nintendo has shown that a true masterpiece can stand the test of time

This remake proves there’s still so much value in the traditional Zelda formula: the dense, intimate world of Hyrule is stuffed with charming characters and fascinating secrets

And finally, just in the interest of showing the odd lower score out there, RPG Site awarded the remake an 8/10:

While some decisions and directions in this remake may keep me from reaching for it again anytime soon, Ocarina of Time is a classic tale and remains a standout among the pantheon of the Zelda titles, and this remake is a great showing of why, even with its blemishes

What a stellar showing, eh? As it stands, the game sits at an eye-watering score of 96 on Metacritic based on 81 critic reviews. Good grief.

#4157. Zelda Ocarina Remake Producers Talk Changing And Maintaining The Game, Easter Eggs, The Bombchu Bowling Alley Operator, And More

Today marks the release of the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2. You can read my full, positive review here. Ahead of the game’s release, but after having played the game to completion (well… 99% as you will learn below), I traveled to New York to speak with Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma (whose work on the original Ocarina of Time marked his first involvement with the series) and Ocarina of Time remake producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi (director of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom among other Zelda titles).

Topics include how the team approached remaking Ocarina of Time, what needed changing and what needed to stay the same, their thoughts on the Easter Eggs from the original game, the fate and marital status of the Bombchu Bowling girl, and more.

The discussion covers a fairly faithful remake of Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64, which launched nearly 30 years ago, but I have spoiler-marked certain questions and answers that might be considered sensitive if you want to maintain surprise when playing the remake yourself.

Mr. Fujibayashi, what is your relationship to Ocarina of Time?

Fujibayashi: Regarding the original Ocarina of Time, at the time I was working for a different company, so it was mainly me as an end user trying to looking forward to the experience of what a 3D Zelda is going to look like. So, really, I was just waiting in anticipation for that.

How long has the remake been in development?

Aonuma: It's actually kind of hard to say exactly when development began because the earliest thought process was us thinking about the 40th anniversary of The Legend of Zelda approaching, and so we started to have this conversation, “Oh, what should we make to mark this occasion?” And then at that point, we decided on Ocarina of Time, and so a lot of time elapsed from the beginning of that conversation about the anniversary until we got to Ocarina. So it's hard to pinpoint exactly when the development itself began.

Was this a more relaxing game to develop after making Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom back-to-back?

Aonuma: Was it relaxing? That's kind of a hard question to ask. I would say it's more a different style of development. So, if we looked at Tears of the Kingdom, Breath of the Wild, these were created as new games with a very different kind of development cycle. Whereas for a remake like this one, we decided to take an interesting approach, which is to bring in this new younger staff and find out what they would bring to this project in terms of their own experience, their own interpretation as newer staff.

And so my role here was really advising them on this, and it's not always like the development cycle of a new game. But in one sense, the producer has to be careful not to advise too much, to say that you must do it like this. You don't want to prescribe the approach that anyone is going to take. You want to make sure that there's enough space for these younger staff members to have their own interpretation, their own approach to it.

Do you have remake philosophies or rules, like what needs to stay the same and what should change?

Fujibayashi: So, in fact, there were pretty clear kind of rules or guidelines, as you said. First, is because you know, as Mr. Aonuma had mentioned, where he wanted to, the development team was centered around the young directors that took part in this development. And when we first started discussing what kind of game and what kind of approach you wanted to take. One thing that really came through and we clarified was, as you mentioned, what are we going to change and what are we going to keep the same.

And I'll start with what we wanted to change, and that was really to make sure that – because we have the ability to use the latest technology through the Nintendo Switch 2 – there's a lot we can change and improve upon, such as you know obviously things like controls, graphics. We also have a new controller, so that allows for the new camera controls. And we’re really able to fine tune and polish the feel of the game and the there was excitement for all the ways of expression we can provide the player.

But on the other hand, thinking about what we didn't want to change, we were thinking about the creators of the original Ocarina of Time, and what they wanted to convey, the experience that they wanted to provide for users and players through this title. That's something that we wanted to keep intact and that spirit to carry across. And we wanted to make sure that this new game is able to deliver that in the way that we

Aonuma: So speaking as someone who worked on the original Ocarina of Time for Nintendo 64, you always have those moments looking back of, “Oh, you know, I really wanted to do more of this,” or, “I wanted to be able to express this in a different way,” but you're faced with certainly the tech limitations of the time. And I went on from Ocarina of Time to work on other Zelda franchise titles, as well. And with each new title, you're always looking for a new way to express something that may not have been available to you previously. But you always have to keep in mind is what makes a Zelda game special, and how do we protect that? How do we keep that in store for the players, as well. So, on this project in particular, I had to think of that through the lens of how do we protect the things that make it the Zelda Ocarina experience, but also how do I give the freedom to the staff to find their own expression of these ideas? And I think between those two things, we found a really good balance. So I'm very happy about that.

When we interviewed you, Mr. Aonuma, for Game Informer’s Breath of the Wild cover story, Shigeru Miyamoto was present, and he made a joke about the challenge of the water temple. Are you happy with where the Water Temple is now in the remake?

Aonuma: Certainly, looking back on the challenge level of the Water Temple, I think it was hard, but some of that came from the system that we were presenting to players. So, for example, if you look at the way that players used to have to switch to the heavy iron boots so that they could sink in the water, you had to go to a different screen and press the button. But now that we're able to give players a shortcut, single button on the gameplay screen, I think they can get to that more quickly. It's a better experience because they can focus on solving the puzzle rather than having to navigate menus and thinking about that and interrupting the flow of their thought each time.

Another consideration compared to the original is that you couldn't move the camera angle in the original game, and so if you were looking for a certain room in this 3D space relative to where you are now, it was much more difficult to orient yourself and think about the space where that room might exist. So I think those two together, you know, also with the heavy boots being one button press, I think this, for me, is the best version of the Water Temple.

Is the canon of the Zelda timeline considered at all during development? Did you think about adding in Easter eggs that made references to things that would have happened later in the Zelda story? Like Wind Waker taking place after Ocarina of Time, for example.

Aonuma: It's funny because the staff would sometimes ask me about the possibility of including nods to the timeline or references to the other game, and I actually, at the time, would say, "No, let's focus on this game. Let's make this the best version of Ocarina of Time that we can." So, the timeline was in the back of our mind, but we didn't consider taking an approach to this game where we actually, explicitly included references like that.

When testing the game, was it challenging to find people who had never played Ocarina of Time?

Aonuma: As it turns out, both on our staff and in the testing teams, there's a lot of young people, and many of them had never played the original. So it wasn't a challenge to find them.

Who do you primarily consider this remake to be for? New people who have never played Ocarina? Or fans like myself who consider it to be, frankly, their favorite game. Who is the important audience?

Fujibayashi: The answer is both. Our response to those fans who have fond memories of this title is really what I mentioned earlier: being able to provide the experience of what it was like to play Ocarina of Time back to them, and that was our response to them. And when it comes to the players that are experiencing this for the first time, whether it's the graphics, or the controls, or the ability to shift and move the camera; those are all changes and fine-tuning that we've made to make sure that people who are used to modern gaming are able to enter this experience with as little friction as possible. So again, to answer your question? It's really both.

Aonuma: Certainly, when you look at the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, there is so much hidden in the world that people spend a lot of time looking for things. And your first time playing through, you may not find all of it in one go. People in that kind of situation would refer to strategy books and information that they can find.

For example, when you're looking for the like last Skulltala and you already have 99, our job is to think about how to give the player an approach to that sort of a problem. What kind of information can we give them to help out. To make it a fun, but still challenging experience, because we want even new players to come in and to be able to fully experience this world that we've created for them, even though old fans are going to come in with a little bit of an advantage in the form of a lot of prior game knowledge.

I'm not kidding about needing some help with that final Skulltala. I'm going to hand you my Switch 2 after this so you can show me where it is because it's been driving me crazy. I've been having dreams about where the final Skulltala might be.

The end of the game in the remake made me emotional in a way I wasn't expecting. It made me cry, just the whole ending of the experience overall. Were you expecting that kind of reaction from players?

Fujibayashi: So first, I want to say I'm very, very happy and excited to hear you say that because, as you mentioned, that cutscene – cutscenes in general – but that cutscene specifically is something that we, as a dev team, heavily discussed. Because of the limitations of the technology back in the day, there might have been things that we weren't able to convey fully, whether it's because of the tempo of the game… whatever it is. And so, when we approached this remake, we wanted to make sure that we captured that moment in the way that we wanted to express it. So that the right kinds of emotions are evoked, and that we can convey the emotion and the story that we wanted to at that moment. And now that hearing you say that and kind of having that reaction really struck a chord? I'm really relieved to hear that because that's exactly what we wanted to do.

The ReDeads, the Shadow Temple, the Dead Hand miniboss, Wall Masters – these enemies traumatized a whole generation of kids. I'm curious if that was always the intention and how did you approach making sure that those elements still remained scary? Was there a line that was too scary?

Aonuma: Certainly, at the time, we had this intent to make sure that we allow the players to find the enemies a little bit scary. They have to be, right? We want to express that sort of thing. But more than anything, they are part of this Fantasy world, which has both light and dark portions, and so we're trying to bring that feeling across. It’s not that we're trying to scare people outright as the entire intent, but rather show that you know Link is part of a brighter part of the world where people are friendly, and Ganon is a part of the darker part of the world where there's a lot of scary things. And we kept that in mind in the remake as well.

We wanted to make sure we were bringing that out, but the tools that we have available to us now for expression are so capable that if we really tried, of course, we could make something that was very, very scary. But this is supposed to be for all kinds of players. We didn't want to hit the scary notes so strongly that we were putting off new players or younger players, and so we want to have that tuning very carefully in mind as we're making those adjustments in terms of presenting that final expression in the game.

I shudder to visualize what the scarier versions of the ReDeads might look like.

Aonuma: What was your experience of them this time?

Oh, terrifying! That noise. The noise they make. That scream. I feel it in my chest. It just recalls that scariness of my childhood in a way that I admit is very entertaining, and I like. Do you remember recording that sound effect? How did you do that? Did you have someone scream?

For the remake, a lot has been rewritten. The meaning hasn't been changed dramatically, but pretty much everything has been rewritten. What was the goal with the rewriting overall?

Fujibayashi: Yes, it's as you said. We did a lot of rewriting of the text. When it comes to the original Ocarina of Time, there's the idea that because it was 28 years ago – it's a long time ago – there's the turn of phrase, or the way it's been written, is sometimes not clear or doesn't work in the modern day, given the context of the modern day. And so that's why we wanted to make sure that it makes sense and it's easier to understand for people who are familiar with playing modern games, and also that it works better here.

And when you think about… obviously the graphics have been improved significantly. Before we had to do things like… “That blue ocarina that is the size that you could fit on a hand,” something like that, to make sure that the idea gets across to the player. But now, because the graphics are improved, it's very clear what the size it is. It's very clear that it's a blue ocarina. So with the new graphics, if you go through the wordy explanation of what it is, the player is going to be like, "Yeah, I can see it." So in order to make sure that we remove those kind of slight hurdles and really make sure that we can present the game and improve not only the expression but also the pacing of the game? That's something that we really took into consideration as we were rewriting the game.

I wanted to ask about some specific changes for the remake. You get five bottles now. Why?

Aonuma: Because bottles are so important to the way the player plays the game, like looking for strategies to deal with different kinds of situations, even at the time of development of the original title, I thought, “Oh, you know, I could do with even just one more bottle.” I think certainly when you collect all four in the original, you feel great about that at time. But I was still thinking like one more would be okay, right?

So, all this time that was in the back of my mind. But when the new younger staff were familiarizing themselves with the old game and thinking about what they might want to change in this version, one thing that I suggested was that the player could get their first bottle earlier, and this would actually be really useful in terms of reinforcing for the player how helpful bottles were and motivating them on their quest to find the next bottle. It strengthens that whole sequence through the game by changing the order just a little bit there. But yeah, certainly, once you have a certain number of bottles, you're going to feel a little bit more confident and more comfortable. But reinforcing that feeling early on, I think, was important for us in the development of this one.

In the original, there were Nintendo character portraits in Zelda's courtyard of Mario, Yoshi, and more, but those have been removed. I was curious as to why.

Aonuma: Certainly, at the time, when we put those there, I don't think anybody thought it was too big a deal. Maybe there was a more carefree or comfortable approach to that sort of thing. But looking at it now, like if a player is coming through that area, and given the overall way that we're, you know, creating this world and giving the player that form of expression, if they look up and they think, "Why is Yoshi there?” We don't want that moment to interrupt their experience of the world in that way. So we're feeling a little bit differently about it this time.

However, you will remember that there is one design element on Talon with Bowser on it, and that's part of the original design of the character. So we didn't change that. That stays as is.

I have some short-answer questions. The woman who runs the Bombchu Bowling game. What happened to her after seven years. And is she single?

Aonuma: That's something we're not going to touch, and I'll leave it to your imagination.

One of the Skulltala rewards is Bombchus, which I found disappointing when I was young, and I found disappointing as an adult. Why does he give you Bombchus?

Aonuma: So that feeling you had when you got, as a reward for a certain number of Skulltalas, the Bombchus, and you thought, “Wait, that's it?” That's also part of the original experience of the 64 version. So there, there's an approach that we take where we try to keep all of the different notes that people felt in the original game in place. You know, sometimes it's really remarkable, fun things, and other times it's slight moments of disappointment. Even that could be memorable in that way. It's important to maintain that.

The Great Fairies. What do they need rupees for?

Fujibayashi: You know, it's really about a feeling. It's like in Japan sometimes, like donations to a temple or something similar like that. It's to express your reverence for the great fairies.

The 3DS remake had Skyward Sword art hidden in a couple of places, but you removed it for this remake. You didn't want to keep the Skyward Sword art?

Aonuma: [Laughs] I do remember at the time the designers on the 3DS version were really interested in placing Easter Eggs like that throughout the game, and the timing of the release of Skyward Sword was such that it was perfect to go ahead and include that. So I said, “Okay, sure.” But like earlier when we were talking about in the courtyard sequence with the Yoshi portrait. You know, you don't want to interrupt the player's experience by seeing something that's unrelated to what they're currently doing in the game. So for that reason, we decided not to go that way.

Mr. Fujibayashi, you directed Skyward Sword. Were you sad to see that reference removed?

Fujibayashi: [Laughs] No, it’s really as Mr. Aonuma said. There was an underlying concept in what we were going for, so no hard feelings there.

I think the biggest cutscene change in the game is when Link transitions from child to adult. It is now a much more involved sequence. Why did that scene need such a drastic change?

Aonuma: So I think that's really connected to the way we were thinking about expressing things in the original. We couldn't do everything. We couldn't express everything that we'd like to, and I think in that moment where you have Ganondorf having this reaction to Link becoming older, that cutscene in the original, it was very low on explanation.

So, you have these thoughts in the player's mind like, “Oh wait, why is he there? What's the relation to this process?” So, you want something that explains his presence, that explains his reaction to make a bigger impression on the player overall, and that's something that you can use to connect the motivation to want to face Ganondorf in the final fight. Something that I think comes across better now.

[I pulled out my Switch 2 and showed them how I was missing one Skulltala in Hyrule Field]

You can see here I have 99 out of 100 and am missing two out of three in Hyrule Field. Can you point to a general location to give me an idea of where to look?

#4156. Former Xbox COO Issues Lengthy Departure Statement To 'Set The Record Straight'

"This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end."

This time last week, we mentioned how newly-promoted Xbox Chief Operating Officer Helen Chiang was suddenly leaving Microsoft after 21 years, with a suggestion at the time that she may have been "terminated for policy violations".

Chiang has now taken to LinkedIn to share a lengthy departure statement in which she denies she was fired for a policy violation, but nevertheless suggests concerns regarding how certain things were handled in her case.

The statement does the talking for itself, so we'll share it in full down below:

"Clarity is Kindness There has been some speculation about my abrupt departure from Microsoft, including claims that I was “fired for a policy violation”. That’s not accurate and while I won’t turn this into a play-by-play, silence should not be mistaken for agreement. What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize. It’s important to me to set the record straight. First, I did not leak confidential company information to the press. I have never communicated with any journalist outside the limited, company-authorized interviews I’ve done as part of my job. That includes every journalist who reached out this week seeking my side of the story. Second, I did not leave XBOX to join a competitor. You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build. XBOX was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here. Third, I did not engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity. I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career. I won’t let speculation define my character or erase that record. Lastly, I did not leave because I was passed over for a bigger role. Since having children, I’ve been intentional about how I define ambition and success. I haven’t actively sought out bigger roles or increased responsibilities, and the last time I interviewed for a job was in 2011. My reputation and results paved the way for the opportunities that followed. I went where the company believed I was needed and where I could have the greatest impact. I did not ask for my most recent role, either. I was promoted into it in July. I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously. I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind. To everyone who has reached out with hugs, love, and support: thank you. So many of you have reminded me of the wonderful times we’ve shared over the past 20 years and the impact we’ve had on one another. Some of you I haven’t been in touch with for several years, yet you still took the time to check on me. Others are people I’ve never even met, but you reached out anyway. That speaks volumes about the care and humanity in our industry and the connections that transcend where we work. This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end. And it is not the whole story."

As you can see, Chiang starts her statement here with the phrase "clarity is kindness", which is a phrase that Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has used on numerous occasions since taking her role a few months ago.

Nothing specific is said about why Chiang was let go (or potentially decided to leave) as part of this statement though, and while she's certainly assertive in getting her point across, there's no evident malice directed at anyone.

Ultimately, she says she's publishing this statement to avoid being linked to "incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal", and that her story is about "staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard".

On behalf of everyone at Pure Xbox, we wish Chiang all the best in her future endeavours.

#4155. Diablo 4’s Warlock looks like an unhinged Necromancer with Sorcerer energy in first look at gameplay

Diablo 4's practitioner of forbidden arts, The Warlock, has been officially unveiled as the second class coming with Lord of Hatred.

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Update, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside new Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.

#4154. "Worth Your Time" - Digital Foundry Delivers Its Tech Review For Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Reviews for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time are live, and that includes a tech-focused assessment from John Linneman over at Digital Foundry.

Naturally, Linneman heaps praise upon Nintendo's remake, with really only a couple of minor nitpicks. To start, resolution ranges from 1080p up to 1440p when docked and from 720p to 1080p during handheld mode. It's noted that handheld mode does implement some tweaks such as more aggressive level-of-detail distances and texture downgrades, but it's overall a very crisp, handsome game.

As for upscaling, Nintendo has seemingly implemented FSR over DLSS. While this isn't a particularly disappointing development, Ocarina of Time does suffer from instances of shimmering, which we noted in our review.

Frame rate, however, is very impressive. While the original was a paltry 20fps (which, to clear, was absolutely fine at the time) with the 3DS remake upping this to 30fps, the Switch 2 remake guns for 60fps and hits it consistently. There may be some "very tiny loading hiccups" here and there, but it otherwise remains stable throughout.

Linneman highlights a bunch of other neat little flourishes, including the fog effects seen in environments along with the lighting from the lava in the Fire Temple. Overall, it's a stunning game, and certainly one of Nintendo's best efforts when it comes to raw presentation and performance.

#4152. Marathon launch player numbers are about half those of the Server Slam, at least on PC

Marathon hasn't quite been able to attract the same volume of players the recent Server Slam did.

After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially launched. Marathon, the extraction shooter from the studio behind Destiny, has managed to find a decent, if a little small of an audience.

The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.

Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.

The open test was largely well-received, and players actually showed up for it. It peaked at a very respectable 143,621 concurrent players on Steam, which put it within striking distance of the peak concurrent of its chief competitor, Arc Raiders - at least when you compare both of their pre-launch Server Slam events.

In Arc Raiders’ case, those figures were far outpaced at the game’s actual launch, and the Embark shooter continues to command a very active player base to this day. A paid product garnering far more players than the same product’s own free sampler is never not a good sign, so many hoped something similar would happen with Marathon.

Marathon has now officially launched, and it doesn’t look like it managed to pull an Arc Raiders - at least so far. At its peak, the Bungie shooter attracted 88,337 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), which is a little over half of its Server Slam’s 143,621 peak concurrent.

Numbers have, of course, dropped since then, which is normal, as players log off for the night. This is obviously not the end of the road for Marathon. Friday, and the weekend, may well push numbers closer to the Server Slam heights.

Indeed, word of mouth is quite positive, with the game currently sitting at a Very Positive user review rating on Steam, based on over 4,600 reviews. As has been proven time and time again in recent years, nothing catapults a game like players emphatically advocating for it to their friends, so it could simply be that mainstream players are cautious.

It will become clear where things settle over the weekend.

#4150. Nioh 3 patch finally makes summons useful in boss fights, brings free armour for everyone

There's a new Nioh 3 patch out in the wild, and it's one that any player who regularly summons in boss fights will really appreciate.

Team Ninja continues to work on Nioh 3. The developer has been releasing regular updates for the action RPG since its launch in early February. Earlier patches have addressed major bugs like healing item use inconsistencies, and more have arrived since to tackle various balance and loot-related issues.

Today’s patch, version 1.04, is a major one, coming in at well over 1GB. There’s plenty here worth getting excited about, so let’s dig in.

To begin with, this is the patch that adds the promised free armour sets for both Ninja, and Samurai. When Nioh 3 reached one million sales, Team Ninja said it would gift every player the Thunderous set in celebration, and the set’s two variants are now available in-game.

The more interesting side of the patch is, unsurprisingly, its change log. There appears to be a focus on online co-op and AI summons in this one, with various tweaks to the make the process more rewarding, and, in some cases, worthwhile.

The amount of Glory obtained when you complete a mission in multiplayer has been increased, regardless of which player was the host. The other major change mainly affects AI Benevolent Grave summons, making it so bosses will no longer target a single player for almost the entirety of the fight.

While summoning AI helpers has always been useful in Nioh 3, they didn’t always help in boss fights, specifically because the boss tended to focus on the player who summoned them, leaving the AI to run around eating AoE hits before dying.

Patch 1.04 makes a couple of welcome gameplay tweaks to the feel of combat. Ninjutsu, and Onmyo Magic will now hit their targets more consistently in situations where there’s a difference in elevation between the player and the enemy.

In the same vein, you’ll now be able to attack (quick/strong) right after jumping, which removes the pause that previously buffered the attack instead. This could mean even more air combos that don’t specifically require Martial Arts.

You can look forward to a couple of quality of life tweaks in this patch, too, such as the change that allows the game to automatically send any Sudama Soul Cores dropped by merchants to your item box. This happens from the second one onwards, which means you won’t have to pick half a dozen each time you go to sell a batch of items.

Speaking of the item box, the limit of forging materials has been increased for some of them. If you’ve been running Battle Scroll missions and Expeditions for gear, you’ll be happy to know that you can now exit the session from the main menu directly.

There’s plenty more to patch 1.04, including fixes and balance tweaks for several weapons, such as Samurai dual swords, odachi, and more for a few Ninja weapons, too. The patch also brings several bug fixes to the game.

You can read the full set of patch notes on Steam.

#4149. Ocarina Of Time Remake Tops Metacritic's GOTY List, And It's High On The All-Time Ranking

Just in case you missed it, the Ocarina of Time remake reviews are in, and they are really rather positive. They are so positive, in fact, that the game has shot straight to the top of Metacritic's Best Games of 2026 list, and it's placing comfortably high on the site's all-time rankings.

At the time of writing, the game has a Metascore of 96 based on 81 critic reviews. This has bumped down the previous gold medallist, Sektori, into second, with a score of 93. Resident Evil 2: Deluxe Edition follows in third, also with 93, with The Witcher III: Wild Hunt - Remaster (92) and Big Walk (91) rounding out the top five.

It's an impressive start for the remake, no doubt, but arguably even more impressive is where it already sits on the Metacritic all-timers list. As it stands, OoT on Switch 2 is ranked Metacritic's 27th best game of all time, slotting in above the likes of Skyrim, Half-Life and even other series entries like Tears of the Kingdom and Wind Waker.

The original Ocarina of Time still sits comfortably in the top spot with a Metascore of 99 (the only game to achieve such an accolade), but considering that every game ranked 34-16 on the list has a 96 score, there's every chance that the remake will move up (or down) as more reviews come in and switch up the order.

And for those wondering, yes, this makes OoT the site's highest-rated Switch 2 game to date, beating out Tears of the Kingdom - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition (95), Hades II (95) and Breath of the Wild - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition (94).

How long OoT remake can retain its position at the top of the 2026 table is another question entirely. To address the neon-soaked elephant in the room, Grand Theft Auto VI is only two weeks away, and we struggle to remember a game ever launching with as much hype. There's every chance that Rockstar's latest might not be quite as well-received as Ocarina, but if anything is going to knock it off the pedestal, it'll be GTA.

#4148. Mass Effect 3 ending discourse ignored the RPG's scale, ambition, and exuberance, including that of its oddly great co-op

Ah, come on, it was fine. Better than fine. We can argue for another fourteen years about whether BioWare should have redone the ending or not, but Mass Effect 3 was really a compendium of endings, a ludicrously ambitious wrapping-up of dozens of plot threads, character arcs, and running gags. Even if you can point to other RPGs that, on an individual basis, are more branching and reactive, Mass Effect 3's largely successful closing of a galaxy's worth of choose-your-own adventure books - filled in and followed across three evolving instalments - showed an audacity and grandiosity that no other three-part series had matched before. Or, at least on that scale, has pulled off since.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

It didn't hurt that Mass Effect 3 also had the trilogy's fiercest, bangiest action by far, nor some of its highest-stakes, often most lip-chewing moments of decisionmaking. It is true that the accumulation of War Assets wasn't always as heavy on character drama as the game-long preparation for Mass Effect 2's Suicide Mission, but then you don't simply play Mass Effect 3 to make a number go higher. You play it to punch or hug reporters, to love or shoot your friends, to save or damn entire species. And it has loads of that, right up to the point to have to choose the colour of an explosion. Potentially beyond, if you treat the (assuredly, delightfully) fanservice-forward Citadel expansion as Shepard's true last ride.

Back in 2013, and again with 2021's Legendary Edition, I was sad that Mass Effect 3 ended and glad that it happened. That, at the risk of appearing less furious at EA's stewardship than I am, does not change with BioWare's closure. What does bother me is the uncertainty over what now happens to Mass Effect 3's surprisingly entertaining, weirdly long-lived co-op mode.

I don't doubt this was put in for boring, C-suite, "gamers want multiplayer" reasons. But that only gave the resultant palled-up superpower maelstroms a sense that they were better than they had any right to be, with explosive moments of player-to-player power synergies and spacious, blindspot-filled maps that could maintain a thrilling feeling of being permanently surrounded. Post-release additions to the species-spanning character roster also showed glimpses of that same, fuck-it swagger that BioWare exhibited in the campaign, as they increasingly moved away from familiar soldier archtypes towards electric whip wielders, regenerating lizards, teleporting ninjas, and three-foot-tall psychic asthmatics. While many of today's co-op shooters fret over miniscule balance changes, in pursuit of some mythically perfect meta, Mass Effect 3's gave you a crate of action figures and told you to go nuts.

While I haven't played it recently, there's a small but loyal contingent who do, and for their sake I hope the multiplayer's P2P setup helps it survive the EA cull. I was, and for now technically still is, too good to be doomed to oblivion. Or, worse, vibe-coded Legendary Edition mods.

#4147. The Sims 4 patch makes it so your public lot gatherings won't be interrupted by rogue Sims

Stranger Sims will no longer just crash your public lot events in The Sims 4 to talk about whatever.

The Sims 4 will soon get a new update to resolve a number of issues, some of which have long caused headaches for players. The latest update will arrive March 17 on PC and Mac, followed by PlayStation and Xbox at an unspecified time later.

Outside of the fixes themselves, the patch also makes good on the recent re-commitment to continue improving quality of life for players, so there’s plenty here longtime players will appreciate.

In the latest episode of The Sims 4’s Laundry List blog series, where the developer goes through the most reported problems with the game and how it plans to solve them, we got a rundown of what to expect from next week’s patch.

You can look forward to five major fixes in this one, but arguably the most important is a change to how Sims determine who they speak with on a lot. This is especially relevant for public lots, where Sims would sometimes interrupt ongoing conversations by barging in and starting a conversation with your Sim.

Going forward, Sims will prioritise familiar Sims with whom they already have rapport, and be less likely to latch onto strangers. If you’ve witnessed a date your Sim was on get interrupted because of that, you’ll certainly appreciate the change.

Speaking of budding romance, Prom is coming back to in-game Calendars, and Sims can once again attend. Maxis said this will work with new and existing saves, and that you should also expect Prom goals to be completable once again.

Pets and animals get some love in this patch, too. First, pets and horses will no longer get lost in Premade Households. The fix prevents that from happening in new saves, but if you already had that happen to you in your current save, it’ll still be there.

You may now also assign animals to an Animal Shed after moving your house to a new lot, so you hopefully won’t be confused as to why they’re stuck in your inventory. This fix applies to existing saves as well as new ones.

Lower down the list of urgent fixes is an update that makes it so Sims’ eye blinking will show fully closed eyes for most interactions. The upcoming patch also comes with a host of Sims autonomy fixes, including one that prevents them from excessively flirting with each other.

Catch up on the full list at the link near the top of the page. And, in case you missed it, Maxis recently announced that The Sims 4 will soon get paid mods, something that many in the community are skeptical about.

#4146. South Of Midnight Director Reflects On Why He Was 'Always Worried' About Funding At Xbox

"It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable."

We absolutely loved South of Midnight when it launched last year as an Xbox first-party title from Compulsion Games, and it's still one of our favourite Xbox Game Studios releases of recent years. However, a year later, Xbox has parted ways with the development team and helped transition them back to an independent studio.

In a nutshell, it seems Xbox wasn't happy enough with South of Midnight's performance from a revenue standpoint, and the same could be said for other smaller releases last year like Double Fine's Keeper and Kiln.

Some fans had been voicing their concerns prior to these releases that Xbox might be putting too much funding into them, and speaking on a recent podcast, South of Midnight director David Sears admitted that he was "always worried" that the funding situation might change and cause Xbox to "close the floodgates".

Here's an excerpt from the MinnMax podcast in which he said this:

"I mean, [Xbox] were funding a lot of games. They were also funding a lot of studios that, you know, I was like, well, okay, great. I guess you have infinite money. Like I was saying earlier, I don't want to feel the weight of the obligation of giant budget or an army of 600 to be responsible for. I want to make something that isn't going to bankrupt Microsoft, I guess, or the games division."

"So, you know, on one hand, if everyone you're working with is either trying to make generational games at not a huge expense, or games that have huge or really significant contemporary commercial appeal, great. It's going to work. But when does that ever happen?"

"I literally told people, 'Wow, this could be terrible.' Because somebody is going to say one day, 'We're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream."

Perhaps most shockingly, the director went on to admit that as much as he wanted to make South of Midnight, it perhaps wasn't sustainable from a funding perspective in hindsight, and that a "shocking outcome" seemed inevitable.

"I mean, I wanted to make it. No doubt, and obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else's money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, 'cause I'm not completely selfless. But it just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. So, of course it was going to have a shocking outcome."

"I mean, it's easy to dissect it now. At the time, I would talk to other directors and would be like, 'How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?' And I would always be like, 'For now, right? There's always a night when Rome burns.' And I didn't know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it."

Of course, none of this is to suggest that Sears wasn't proud of South of Midnight, or that he didn't think it was worthwhile, but it just appears he was concerned with the Xbox money was putting into (and expecting back) for it.

Nevertheless, it seems like he had a very positive experience working with Microsoft overall:

"To their credit, it's amazing, right? I think there's definitely corporate Microsoft DNA but they're vastly different from the Microsoft I knew back in the '90s or the early 2000s, right? Much more humane, actually. It's remarkable and commendable."

"Working on South of Midnight, it became clear to me - some games, their time is not on release. Some games are generational, right? Something that has a good message or is transportive to places that will remain timeless will endure and audiences will find them."

His prediction did ultimately come true - Xbox decided to "close the floodgates" earlier this year by splitting from multiple studios including Compulsion Games, and seemingly adopting a new strategy of focusing on their core franchises like Halo, Forza, Gears, Fallout and others.

We're just pleased that Compulsion Games didn't end up getting closed altogether, and that South of Midnight did actually see the light of day instead of being cancelled during development. We reckon it could end up being one of those Sunset Overdrive-style titles in the future - a cult classic that people end up really enjoying from years past.

We need to consider that Game Pass is massive revenue, but it also needs to be adjusted to optimise global revenue with behemoths like Call of Duty. Asha announced adjustments and modular plans, and she also reduced the price of Ultimate. She removed day one Call of Duty and unlimited Cloud. Matthew and her want people to pay exactly for what they want, without making the subscription too expensive, and that's the best outcome, because it's better business for them, while players only pay for what they want, even if they are paying more for each thing, e.g., day one and Cloud. This is the way that I think Game Pass makes total sense.

In this long-term business context, day one inclusions should be a more expensive add-on, or games should arrive after one year, which is what Premium is. Thus, I think that "Ultimate" will become an expensive add-on, and Cloud already is beyond the included hours. I expect this change in 2027, because she has proven that her strategy is not to raise the general prices nor to try to get extra revenue from PS while alienating the Xbox ecosystem.

So, what Asha and Matthew are doing is to make Xbox (including Xbox on PC) a platform with exclusives, while making Game Pass more profitable, but also more flexible and accessible. Besides, reducing the bloated infrastructure and letting studios like The Compulsion go is the only way to protect that profitability.

#4145. I've got egg on my face because Steam's Personal Calendar feature has apparently been a test this whole time and is only now actually a fully fledged component

I'll be honest folks: I didn't know that Steam's Personal Calendar feature was still technically in testing. I've been using it here and there to keep track of what's come out recently or what's coming out imminently, and have generally found it to be fairly reflective of the kinds of games I was interested in. It just worked! Yet lo and behold, a post from Valve went out yesterday announcing that the feature has launched out of Steam Labs "and is considered a full feature of the Steam Store."

The feature, if you've missed it, is "another way to see recommended games for you, showing both recently released and upcoming games filtered down to the set of games we think you are most likely to be interested in," as Valve explain it anyway. "It uses your recently played games to find people with similar playtime profiles to you, and then looks at the games those players have been adding to their wishlist or playing." I do wonder if there's a bit more going under the hood here, as my playtime count is all over the place, with nothing above 50 hours on there, and that's an exception to the norm (I'm from more of a console background, alright).

But even still, my recommendations do remain pretty good, showing me games that I have since added to my wishlist. I'm never opposed to new discovery tools, especially considering how bad Valve can actually be at that kind of thing. Apparently the recommendation system refreshes daily "to incorporate the latest data. In reality you aren't likely to see your recommendations change all that much from day to day, but as time goes by you will obviously see new things pop up as the 8-week horizon of the calendar marches forward, or as games lock in their release dates."

This comes as part of a broader swathe of changes Valve have been introducing to Steam over the past couple of years, including one from last month that will change its homepage discounts and events section to be a bit more algorithm based. Perhaps it's some kind of weird prepwork for that new Half-Life they're almost definitely making but only talk about accidentally.

#4144. Crimson Desert PC specs don't keep resolution and framerate targets a secret, and they don't use upscaling for everything either

Finally, a PC specification list that actually indicates resolution and framerate targets, and doesn't leave console players behind.

Crimson Desert is a little over one week away from release, and developer Pearl Abyss has delivered the official, final list of specs for the game. The twist is that the specs not only include useful information for PC players, they also cover similarly relevant details for console players, who traditionally don’t get mentioned in those reveals.

The specs are decently detailed, but more surprisingly - except for a single instance - they don’t include upscaling on PC, another thing games have gotten too comfortable using, even with their lowest specs.

On the official Crimson Desert website, developer Pearl Abyss has delivered a chunky post breaking down five different sets of PC requirements for the upcoming open-world action RPG. Each set indicates the graphics preset being used - and crucially, the resolution and framerate targets you can expect with each.

With the exception of the Minimum spec, all other presets do not appear to rely on upscaling of any kind. They do not say, however, whether ray tracing is being used with any of them, which is a feature that will throw all of those specs out of whack.

That same transparency also extends to non-PC platforms, which traditionally get few, if any, details about their own resolution and framerate targets. The console set of specs are extensive, just like PC, covering both PlayStation, and Xbox.

It’s granular enough to indicate which upscaling tech is being used, where applicable. This is relevant for owners of a PS5 Pro, a console that has access to Sony’s PSSR upscaling, alongside the standard AMD FSR tech the base console - and Xbox - use.

The developer has also revealed the base resolution for each mode across each console, and the resolution the image will be upscaled to using whichever tech is being utilised.

And, if you’re one of the five people who play games on Mac, you’ll be thrilled to know that the specs also include a section for Mac devices, split between the different Mac chips. The quality preset being used with each is not clear, however.

Finally, there's a set of specs for the Rog Xbox Ally, covering both the X and S models.

Crimson Desert arrives March 20 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. You can expect more coverage from us at release and beyond.

Those after even more Pokémon Pokopia content need not wait too much longer, as The Pokémon Company has announced that the game's second wave of DLC will launch next month on 9th December.

The 'Dazzling Decorations' DLC isn't quite as big as its Bubbly Basin predecessor, but it's still a very cute addition for all those who are after a little bit of 'mon customisation. The biggie this time around is a bunch of new accessories that you can stick on Ditto and your Poké pals. Did you need to see Dedenne in a pair of shades? This is the pack for you.

A few new Pokémon are included in this one, too with the likes of Skitty, Doduo, Sylveon and more all joining the fray.

Here are a few adorable snaps, so you know what to expect:

While we're a little disappointed that the second wave won't pack in another new biome, TPC has promised that there's more of that to come in Wave 3, which is set to launch at some point next year.

Remember, you'll need to have rebuilt your first Pokémon Center and completed the 'Raise the environment level' and 'Find a doll' Withered Wasteland requests before you can dive into the DLC.

#4142. Xbox Set A New Record For Game Releases In October, With Extremely Impressive Support For Play Anywhere

It's no secret that a whole bunch of new releases have been moving their release dates from November back to September and October in recent months, and it's actually resulted in a new record being set for Series X and S in 2026.

As shared by the folks behind the Xbox news for Koreans account on social media, there were 208 games released across Xbox Series X and S (and Xbox One in some cases) in October 2026, which represents the "peak month" for this year. September is second with 187 releases, and April is third with 169 releases.

Of those 208 games last month, 45% were Xbox Play Anywhere enabled, which is a pretty incredible percentage!

As you can see, the Play Anywhere percentage has been as high as 50% in 2026, and it's raised quite considerably compared to the figures we were seeing in the first few months of the year.

This clearly indicates that Xbox is ramping up the push to get as many games as possible integrated into the programme, and we're here for it - it's always incredible to get a free PC copy on top of your Series X and S purchase!

November will be much quieter for new releases with GTA 6 hogging the spotlight of course, and December should see things slow down considerably as well. As we approach the new year though, it looks like we can expect well over 1,000 new releases on Xbox Series X|S in 2027 once again, with maybe around half of them getting Xbox Play Anywhere support along the way. Bring it on!

#4141. Paralives' first major update slips to next year, but when it comes you can expect some pretty meaty improvements for all of its main features

Since launch back in May of this year, life sim Paralives appears to have been trucking along nicely, with the dev team offering up fairly regular updates with all sorts of tweaks big and small. Certainly confidence-inspiring for an early access game, especially one as systems-driven as it is. And now, the Paralives team have outlined their plans for the game's first major update, which seem very catered to improving the core experience.

As part of a four point plan they outlined, first up on the docket is "buffing up the basics." This is all about strengthening some of the currently existing Live Mode systems. That means improvements to how relationships function by unlocking more things when a relationship level goes up, adding in more interactions that change your Para's emotions, improving the Community Centre's bundles and tweaking the economy curve so it isn't as easy to get money.

The next point is on expanding the Live Mode, meaning the addition of a pair of new skills, adding in more together and story cards, new relationship label unlockables, and more jobs too. Build Mode will also see some improvements, with a big focus on build breaking bugs. You can also expect new bits of furniture and items, and a tweak to furniture and item efficiency.

Lastly, there are also planned improvements to the Paramaker. One is by adding in more hairstyles and clothing items, notably baggy outfits, and the other is increasing the range of fat and muscle sliders "to represent a wider variety of body shapes." As a bigger person myself I'm always enthused when character creators actually let you have a fat body, so this is a welcome point from the dev team.

Worth noting that this list "is not final," and some things may be pushed back with others getting added in. Also worth noting is that while this first major update was planned for the end of 2026, it's been pushed into next year as the team needs a bit more time. You can read about all of these plans in more detail over on Steam.

#4140. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with a decent selection of maps and modes

Battlefield 6's second-ever free trial, and the first in 2026, is upon us.

Battlefield Studios has announced that Battlefield 6 is going free to play for one week next week. Well, a portion of the game is, anyway, as part of a free trial that will include some of the game’s most popular modes and maps.

Though it does not encompass the entirety of the game, the free trial is fairly generous. Here’s what to expect.

For starters, the trial kicks off Tuesday, March 17 and will run until the following Tuesday, March 24. The trial will be accessible from Battlefield Redsec, the already free-to-play portion of the game.

Once downloaded, you’ll find a new Battlefield 6 Free Trial section in the main menu. Because Redsec and Battlefield 6 multiplayer share progression, if you played the former at any point, you’ll be able to pick up from where you left off.

The same is also true the other way around; if this is your first time with Battlefield 6, all your unlocks will carry over to the full version, as well as to Redsec if you decide stick with the free-to-play off-shoot.

Once it kicks off, you’ll find three playlists to choose from. Casual Breakthrough, All-out Warfare, and a third playlist showcasing the new Nightfall game mode and its associated map.

All-out Warfare is what you come to Battlefield for, and that playlist features Conquest, Breakthrough, as well as BF6’s newcomer Escalation - all large-scale, combined arms game modes. They will be playable across four maps. You get to play on two from Season 2: Contaminated, and Hagental Base, one from Season 1: Eastwood, and Mirak Valley from the base game.

Casual Breakthrough is based on a playlist that already exists in the core game, and it’s really designed as a nice on-ramp for new players. It also offers less intense gameplay, perfect for people grinding unlocks.

Casual Breakthrough is limited to just 16 real players (eight per team), with the rest filled up with bots. You earn the same amount of XP in those matches, except when you interact with bots, so killing a bot will net less than a human player. Outside of that, unlocks, Challenges and all other things that don’t depend on stat-tracking can be done within.

In the trial, the Casual Breakthrough playlist includes Hagental Base, Contaminated, and Eastwood.

The most interesting is the third playlist, in part because its content will also be available to owners of the full game for the first time right alongside free-to-play players. Nightfall is a playlist exclusive to the Hagental Base map.

This is a very small map, so the mode selection here is Team Deathmatch, Squad Deathmatch, and Domination. Under Nightfall conditions, lights across the entire map are turned off, so you’re going to have use your NVGs to be able to see. This is also a god opportunity to try out weapon attachments that specifically work under low-light conditions, which typically don’t get much use in multiplayer.

March 17 also marks the launch of the second stage of Battlefield 6’s Season 2, which comes with the aforementioned Nightfall content, as well as a big new update - so the timing works out nicely for everyone.

#4139. South of Midnight's Director Wouldn't Have Funded It, Says Xbox's Approach Was Unsustainable

South of Midnight is the latest title from Compulsion Games, a studio that used to be under Microsoft's umbrella before it reclaimed its independence earlier this year.

It seemingly underperformed, even with ports to other platforms, including PS5, just under a year after its Xbox launch.

Now, in a new interview with Minnmax, the game's director, David Sears, has made new comments about the game and Xbox's funding at the time.

To summarise, he says that, while it was highly commendable of the company to support smaller, higher-risk titles such as South of Midnight and Double Fine's Keeper, it was ultimately unsustainable because the "infinite money" had to stop at some point.

"They were funding a lot of games," Sears says. "They were also funding a lot of studios that, you know, I was like 'well, okay, great, I guess you have infinite money, you do you, I want less. I don't want to feel the weight of the obligation of a giant budget, or an army of 600 to be responsible for. I want to make something that isn't going to bankrupt Microsoft or the games division.'"

"So on one hand, if everyone you're working with is either trying to make generational games at not a huge expense, or games that have huge or really significant contemporary commercial appeal – great, it's going to work. But when does that ever happen, right?"

Sears was "always worried" about South of Midnight suddenly losing funding, suggesting that if he was heading up Xbox, he "probably" would have done exactly that.

"I literally told people, 'Wow, this could be terrible.' Because somebody is going to say one day, 'We're closing those floodgates.' And that's going to have really traumatic results downstream."

"I mean, I wanted to make it, no doubt, right? Obviously, because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else’s money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah, because I’m not completely selfless.

"But, you know, it just seems like in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable, so of course, it was going to have a 'shocking' outcome."

While there have been no official sales figures for South of Midnight, analytical estimates from Alinea back in April 2026 had the PS5 version specifically at about 16,000 sales.

Other data, such as Steam player counts, don't paint a particularly rosy picture either, and Sears' own comments in this interview also suggest it didn't hit its mark.

For a while, Xbox was funding games of all shapes and sizes in order to fill out Game Pass, but this approach, spearheaded by former CEO Phil Spencer, doesn't seem to be in place anymore, with his replacement, Asha Sharma, making severe cuts to get the business back on track.

South of Midnight is a great game, by the way, but if even the director was doubting its commercial potential, it was clearly not going to be a big seller.

#4138. HELENA : Cloud District is a megastructure photography game laser targeted at my interests, and it's out next week

Yes, I'm doing it, I'm writing about a megastructure game for the second time this week because come on, HELENA : Cloud District just looks stunning, don't it? Admittedly there's a chance you've not heard of it, that be the way of things in this algorithmically dominated world, but allow me to tell you about its big, scary world and the strange camera you're equipped with to capture all the sights it holds.

In the world of HELENA : Cloud District, you have come across a rotting megastructure that appears to be long abandoned, all sorts of strange flora dotted throughout it. In one part, it's something of a precision first-person platformer, as you navigate its intricately layered world with drops so steep you'd probably die before you hit the bottom. At the centre of it all is a computer, and it's here where you must bring all of your photographs in order to learn more about the history of the place.

The in-game camera itself is a fascinating thing to look at, completely impossible, alien and ancient in its design. From what I can tell it's a sort of metallic helmet, these insect-like segments snapping into place when you're gearing up to take a snap. You only appear to have three photo slots at any given point in time, meaning you can't just go gallivanting around the place all trigger happy like. There's an amount of care you have to put in positioning yourself and subsequently finding your way back to the central computer.

It's non-linear too, there's no set path you have to take, and it seems like there's some neat movement mechanics too. "Slide, hover, and glide through the structure in your own creative way in order to reach every level and get deeper into the slumbering Cloud District," explains the game's Steam page. Sounds like you don't have to worry too much about that falling to your death thing, then. I'm quite enthused by what HELENA : Cloud District is putting down, and it has a release date now too: October 29th. Same day as Hypnos! I now dub October 29th megastructure day. There will not be a vote on this matter. Ahead of HELENA's release, make sure to give it a wishlist on Steam.

#4137. Kirby Air Riders' Cancelled Halloween Event Gets A Returning Replacement

After cancelling its Halloween event last week thanks to some nasty performance woes, Nintendo has today revealed Kirby Air Riders' replacement event. What's more, it starts today!

This one features a returning ruleset from the Shadow Star's Revenge event (which last appeared in March 2026), though the Ghost headwear reward from the cancelled Halloween event is still in place at 1,100 points — it's never too late to get a little spooky, after all.

This event is going live later today, running from 4th November at 7pm PT (that'll be 5th Nov, for those in Europe) until 9th November at 7pm PT.

While all points redeemed in the short-lived Trick or Treat event have now been reset to zero, Nintendo is increasing the number of points earned per match to make it easier to pick up all the rewards.

Original Story: If you have been keeping up with Kirby Air Riders of late, you might have been excited to dive into the game's new Halloween event this weekend and pick up some spooky Ghost headwear while you're at it. Well, we're sorry, but that's not going to happen, as Nintendo has cancelled the event.

The event was originally scheduled to run from 28th October through until 4th November, but many players reported nasty technical difficulties when taking part in early matches, where the screen would regularly freeze — which, in a game as frantic as Air Riders, isn't going to cut it.

You can see the issue for yourself below (shared on Bluesky by TAHK0):

nintendo just canceled the kirby air riders halloween event (no, seriously) because this kept happening lol

This time, Nintendo didn't have a quick fix up its sleeve, so it decided to cancel the event instead. "We have confirmed an issue in the currently ongoing event 'Trick or Treat!' where the screen temporarily freezes during gameplay," a message from the Japanese Nintendo Support social media account (via machine translation) read this morning. "For this reason, we will be cancelling this event."

While Nintendo went on to apologise for the cancellation, it claimed that there are plans to hold the event again in the future, so everyone can get in on the themed reward. There's no official news on when it will return at the moment, but we have to imagine it will be sooner rather than later.
